activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
story:
The third-floor study room smelled of old carpet and the lemon wipes the janitor used on the tables, and Abigail spread her materials across half of it before her friends arrived: the photocopied case, two legal pads, a bag of clementines for sharing. She had drawn a line down the center of the first pad and written PLAINTIFF on the left and DEFENDANT on the right, because Ms. Dang had pulled her name for petitioner and then, with the unreadable calm of a person dealing cards, assigned her respondent as well. Both sides. One girl, one case, two mouths to feed.

"You look like you're planning a war," Amelia said, dropping her backpack on the chair nearest the radiator. Genevieve came in behind her carrying three hot chocolates from the cart by the front desk, and she set one at Abigail's elbow without being asked, which Abigail noticed, and which she would think about later, the way Genevieve always seemed to know what people needed before they said it.

"Brandenburg," Abigail said. "Clarence Brandenburg, a KKK leader, spoke at a rally with men in hoods, some carrying weapons. He said revenge might be taken. Ohio convicted him under a law against advocating violence. The Supreme Court reversed it in 1969." She tapped the photocopy. "The state argued the speech was dangerous. His side argued it was just words."

"So argue that hate speech is terrible but protected," Amelia said, peeling a clementine.

"It's not that simple, and I have to be respondent too. That's the part that's making me crazy." Abigail pulled the second pad closer. On the mock court's hypothetical, which Ms. Dang had written on the whiteboard downstairs, a speaker at an angry rally had told a crowd to march on a store and take what they were owed, and the crowd had started moving. Abigail read it again, moving her lips. The hypothetical wasn't the real case. It was Brandenburg's shadow stretched onto new facts, and she had to decide how far the shadow reached.

Genevieve leaned over her shoulder. "What's the actual rule, though? From the real one."

Abigail found the sentence in her notes and read it aloud. "Advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action." She said it twice more, slower the second time, because the sentence had a shape and she wanted to feel the hinges of it.

"That's the test," Amelia said. "Imminent lawless action. Say that in the round and you're golden."

"There are pieces, though. Directed to inciting. Imminent. Likely. It's like a gate with three latches, and all of them have to open." Abigail drew three small boxes on the pad and labeled them. "Brandenburg's speech, revenge someday, maybe, to a small crowd of already-committed people, far from any target. The hypothetical speaker says march now, to an agitated crowd, a block from the store. Different words, different moment, different distance. I keep flipping sides and I keep getting different answers, and I can't tell if that means I'm doing it wrong or doing it right."

Genevieve had gone quiet, turning her cup in her hands. When she spoke it was careful, the way she handled breakable things. "Maybe you're supposed to get different answers. That's what arguing is. You're not trying to find the one true side. You're trying to make each side as strong as it can honestly be."

Abigail looked at her. "But at some point I have to decide what I actually think. If the judges ask me which way I'd rule."

"Then decide, and admit what you're unsure about," Genevieve said. "Ms. Dang told me once that the best oralists concede a hard question before the judges ask it. It doesn't make you weaker. It makes you judicious."

Amelia groaned softly. "Genevieve, you just reified my worst fear. Now the round is a real thing with teeth instead of a bad dream I could ignore." But she was grinning when she said it, and she pushed the clementines across the table toward Abigail, who had stopped eating.

Abigail worked for a while without talking. On the petitioner's side she wrote that the hypothetical speech met every latch: the words were aimed at inciting, the lawless action was imminent, and given the crowd's movement it was likely. On the respondent's side she wrote the harder argument, the one she had almost avoided, that the crowd's march proved only anger, not that the speech caused it, that punishing the speaker for what listeners did would let the government silence any agitator on the theory that crowds are unstable. Then, at the bottom of the second pad, under a line she drew with the flat of her hand, she wrote what she herself believed: that the words and the moment mattered together, that a speaker pointing an angry crowd at a store a block away was not Brandenburg, and that if she were a justice she would rule for the state in the hypothetical and still feel the loss of it, because the same rule that protected Clarence Brandenburg, a man whose speech she despised, was the rule she wanted living when she needed it.

She read the page over and found it held an honesty she could stand behind, a position with a seam of doubt showing, not hidden.

"What time is the round?" Amelia asked, gathering the peels onto a napkin.

"Tomorrow, four o'clock. Ms. Dang is presiding." Abigail squared her pads, petitioner on top, respondent beneath, her own small unwritten opinion underneath everything like a foundation. Outside the study room's glass wall, the library was dimming, the lamps on the long tables coming on one by one, and somewhere below them a mother was whispering to a child that it was time to choose one last book.

"Same room after?" Genevieve asked. "We'll run questions at you. Be your detractors."

"Be merciless," Abigail said, and slid the hot chocolate closer, and took her first real sip, still warm.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Canada's 2019 food guide suggests filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grain foods.
story:
William counted the folding tables first, because Ms. Nur had told him the Tuesday crowd could reach sixty and she was never wrong about that. The community kitchen smelled of onions already sweating in a pot someone had started at seven, and the walk-in fridge hummed behind him like a held breath. He was eighteen and this was his job interview, though nobody had called it that; Ms. Nur called it a trial week, and the trial was this: plan meals for seven days, shop for them, cook them in batches, and keep the whole thing under the budget she had written on a receipt in green ink.

"Half," he said to himself at the whiteboard, marker hovering. He had printed Canada's 2019 food guide plate that morning at the library because his phone plan had run out and his mother had said, gently, that she could not top it up this month. The plate was a simple diagram. Half of it was vegetables and fruits, a quarter was protein foods, and a quarter was whole grain foods. He had dismissed it at first as something for children, a poster for a gymnasium wall, but the more he stared at his scribbled list of spaghetti and frozen sausages, the more the proportions rearranged his thinking. If he planned each plate that way, the shopping list almost wrote itself: cabbage, carrots, lentils, a sack of barley, one tray of the discounted chicken thighs the grocery store marked down on Sunday nights.

Jett arrived at nine with a coffee for William and nothing for himself, which William had learned meant Jett's own money had run out by Monday. "You're doing the whole week at once?" Jett said, leaning on the counter, watching William lay out seven metal trays like evidence. "That's insane. That's, like, army stuff."

"It's batch cooking," William said. "Cook once, portion, freeze. Otherwise by Thursday you're eating cereal and lying about it."

"That's literally what I do."

"I know. That's why you're here."

Sarah-Eve came in with the shopping receipts and spread them across the steel counter, and together they checked the arithmetic, and here the problem surfaced, the real one, the one William had been circling all morning. The vegetables ate the budget. Half the plate meant half the money, nearly, and the good produce was not what was cheap; the cheap stuff was the tired stuff, the peppers gone soft, the lettuce that would desiccate into nothing in the walk-in by Wednesday. He had two beliefs pulling in opposite directions and he could feel them pulling. One was the guide's proportions, clean and principled, a rule he could hold onto. The other was the plain fact that Ms. Nur's clients ate first and asked questions never, and that a batch of rice and ground pork would feed more people than a batch of barley and squash.

"So scale up the grain," Sarah-Eve said, practical as a hammer. "Nobody checks a plate with a protractor."

"Somebody should," William said, and then heard how it sounded, and Jett laughed at him, not unkindly, and William laughed too, but he didn't drop it. He stood over the trays and tried to hold both ideas at once the way you hold two groceries in one hand. Maybe the proportions were not a rule but a direction, an arrow rather than a destination. Maybe you built the list toward half vegetables and fruits, a quarter protein foods, a quarter whole grain foods, and where you landed short, you landed short honestly.

Ms. Nur came through at noon, tasted the lentil soup from a wooden spoon, and said nothing for a moment long enough that the kitchen noise seemed to fall to a diminuendo, the dishwasher's spray, the radio in the corner, everything receding while she decided. "The soup is good," she said. "The plan is better. Where did you learn the plate?"

"Food guide," William said. "Canada's, 2019. It's just a picture."

"It's never just a picture." She tapped the shopping list with the spoon. "You went over on vegetables."

"Yes. Nine dollars over. I took it from the grain budget and I'd do it again, but I want to say it out loud first instead of hiding it in the arithmetic."

She looked at him the way teachers look when a student has done the thing they were actually testing for. "Then next week you'll find the produce clearance at the market on Ronald Street, and you'll tell me Monday what it did to the plan."

Jett had been quiet, stacking containers, and when Ms. Nur left he said, "I thought you'd argue with her. You always argue."

"I did argue. I just did it with the budget line." William ladled soup into the first container, and the steam climbed past his face and vanished under the fluorescent light. "Come Thursday, help me carry the squash ones to the freezer."

"Fine," Jett said, "but only because you bought the good bread."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The road out past the grain elevator ran straight for two miles before it bent toward the creek, and Carter's father had chosen it because there was almost nothing to hit. Carter sat behind the wheel with his permit folded in his shirt pocket, his hands at ten and two the way the booklet said, and his father in the passenger seat with one hand braced casually on the dash, which Carter found more unnerving than any instruction. The car rolled forward in first gear, lurched, and died.

"You're letting the clutch up too fast," his father said, in the tone of a man who had decided before they left the driveway to remain calm. "Try it again."

On the fourth attempt the engine caught and held, and the fence posts began to slide past. Carter had waited all winter for this, had studied the manual in the back of Mr. Haile's classroom during study hall while Mr. Haile graded papers and occasionally looked over and nodded. He had a plan, too, the kind a person builds without saying it aloud: get the permit, learn on the old truck, and by June drive Caleb and Rhys to the lake every afternoon, the three of them with the windows down.

That plan collapsed at the general store, four miles out, where they stopped so his father could buy coolant. Rhys was there, leaning against the ice machine with Caleb, both of them having biked out on the long gravel shoulder. "You got it," Rhys said, smacking the truck's fender with an open palm, bellicose in the way he got when he was pleased. "Carter's licensed. Lake run Friday. I'm calling it now."

Carter looked at his father, who was reading the back of the coolant bottle with remarkable attention. "I can't," Carter said. "Not yet. It doesn't work like that."

"Like what? You have the paper."

Carter had read the section twice on the bus, but saying it aloud felt different, like reciting a rule in front of the referee. "There's this thing most places do now. Graduated licensing. You don't just go from permit to full license. First you're on the permit, and you have to have a licensed adult with you. Then you get a provisional license, and that one still has restrictions on it. Only after that do you get the full license." He heard how it sounded, like a fence built specifically around him. "So Friday, no. I can't drive you guys anywhere."

Rhys made a noise of disgust and turned to Caleb as if to share the offense, but Caleb only shrugged. "My cousin's on the provisional one," Caleb said. "She can drive alone but there's a limit on passengers at night. It's not personal, man. They do it to everybody our age."

"They stigmatize us," Rhys said. "That's what it is. Sixteen-year-olds are the one group it's okay to treat like we're radioactive."

"It's not a contrivance aimed at you," his father said mildly, coming over with the bottle. "It's just the system, and it's fairly new, and it's boring, and it will pass." He nodded toward the truck. "Coolant first. Then you're driving us home, and this time you'll find third gear without sounding like you're grinding coffee."

On the way back Carter drove better. The bend by the creek came and went without incident, and he even managed the downshift, hearing the engine settle into a lower, steadier voice. Rhys and Caleb had pedaled off ahead, their bikes small and bright on the shoulder, and he understood that they would go to the lake Friday without him and that this was survivable, though it did not feel entirely fair, and he could not decide whether fairness was even the right measure. A rule that applied to everyone his age still landed on him specifically, here, in June, and both of those things were true at once.

His father pointed at the turn for their road. "Signal early," he said. "Check your mirror."

Carter signaled, checked, and turned in a wide, careful arc, the tires holding the gravel exactly where he intended them to. Ahead, near the mailbox, Caleb and Rhys stood over their bikes, and Rhys lifted both arms in mock salute. Carter slowed, rolled down the window, and called, "Next summer," and Rhys cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted back, "You'd better mean that."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A mortgaged home is collateral for the loan, so if the borrower stops paying, the lender can foreclose, taking and selling the home to recover the debt.
story:
Dylan had expected the apartment to feel like freedom, but the hallway smelled like wet carpet, and the landlord's keys jingled with an impatience that suggested the viewing would last exactly eight minutes. He had saved eleven hundred dollars from two summers at the garden centre, and the deposit, the landlord said over his shoulder, was first and last month's rent, which meant twelve hundred before Dylan even slept there. He did the arithmetic twice while the man opened the blinds with a slap of the cords.

"When can you move in?" the landlord asked. "Someone else looked this morning."

"Can I think about it until tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow, sure. But I can't hold it." The man's tone was friendly the way a checkout line is friendly, and Dylan understood that friendliness was part of the price too.

He had not come alone, exactly. Lexi was waiting on the building's front steps, chin on her knees, having refused to climb to the fourth floor on principle. "Smell it from here," she said. "That's the moribund cigarette smell of a building nobody has loved since 1998."

"It's eight hundred a month, all inclusive."

"It's eight hundred a month to own nothing at the end. My parents did that for ten years and then my dad had a whole speech about it." She stood, dusting off her jeans. "Rent is money that leaves. That's all he ever says."

Dylan had heard his own father's version of the speech, though his came out differently, and Dylan had been thinking about it on the bus over. Four years ago there had been a sign on the lawn two houses down, orange paper stapled to a stake, and he had asked what "foreclosure" meant. He had been fourteen. His father had said, not unkindly, that when you buy with a mortgage the house itself is collateral for the loan, so if you stop paying, the lender can foreclose, taking the house and selling it to recover the debt. That was the whole explanation, and Dylan had watched the neighbours, the ones with the trampoline, carry boxes for a weekend and then not be neighbours anymore.

His father brought it up again last month, at the kitchen table, in the low voice he used for money. He and Dylan's mother had been offered a mortgage renewal at a higher rate, and he was trying to decide whether to stretch for a bigger place, the kind with a yard. "We could be house-poor for five years," he said, "and then fine." He had said "we" but Dylan understood that his own tuition, his bus pass, the eleven hundred dollars, all of it sat inside that sentence like furniture inside a house. His father had never denigrated renting, which Dylan respected; he only said that owning meant the bank could take it if you failed, and renting meant the landlord could take it if you succeeded somewhere else and left. "You're exposed either way," he said. "Different weather."

Eliana, who worked at the credit union after school and had agreed to meet him after the viewing, had a third position, which she delivered while stirring a milkshake she had not ordered for herself. "A down payment is just the entry fee," she said. "You save five, ten percent, you get a mortgage, and now the house is the bank's hostage until you pay it off over decades. People romanticize it. People also romanticize rent control, and neither one is romance." She tapped the table. "What you actually have is eleven hundred dollars and a backpack. So the question isn't owning versus renting. It's what you can afford to lose."

He had wanted, all summer, not to be the person who still lived at home during first year. The want had been physical, a tightness behind his ribs when friends talked about dorms and leases, and he had caught himself denigrating his own neighborhood to make the leaving seem more necessary, calling it dead-end and tiny in conversations where none of that was true. The mendacity of it embarrassed him now, sitting in the booth, because the truth was simpler and harder: he wanted out, and wanting out was not a reason.

Back at the building, because the landlord had left the outer door unlatched, Dylan climbed the stairs alone a second time. He stood in the empty apartment and listened to the refrigerator hum and a neighbour's television laugh at something. He put his hand flat on the counter, which was clean, actually, cleaner than the hallway had promised. Twelve hundred to get in, eight hundred every month after, and nothing owned at the end, but also nothing the bank could seize, no collateral, no stake in the yard. His father's weather. His mother had said once that the neighbours with the trampoline had bought a smaller place and seemed, weirdly, happier, and Dylan had never known whether that was comfort or observation, and he still didn't.

He took a photo of the kitchen on his phone and texted it to his father with no caption, then stood at the window while the three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared. Below him Lexi was pacing the sidewalk on the phone with someone, gesturing at the building as though testifying. The message came back as a single question mark, and after that, a second message: "What's the heat included in?" Dylan smiled at the screen, at the ordinary smallness of the question, and typed back, "I'll ask in the morning."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
Mya had volunteered for the peer health program because Ms. Smith said the juniors trusted students more than pamphlets, and because she wanted to be the kind of person who knew things other people needed. Every Tuesday after last bell she sat in the back corner of the health classroom with Elliana and Isis, practicing on each other. That afternoon the assignment was contraception, and she kept fumbling the order of her sentences. "The IUD is long-acting, the implant is long-acting, the pill is not," she said, and Isis, who had heard it four times, recited along with her mouth full of pretzel.

"You sound like a robot," Elliana said. She was sitting on the radiator under the window, the arboreal shade of the oak outside pressing its leaf shadows against her knees. "Nobody our age says long-acting."

"Nobody our age says anything out loud about this," Isis said. "That's the whole problem."

Ms. Smith had given them a script for the consent lesson too, and Mya had privately decided the script was a bromide, something smooth and obvious, yes means yes, that would evaporate the second it hit a real conversation. She had watched a boy at a party last fall put his hand on a girl's waist and look at her face for a fraction of a second before she moved away, and she had not said anything, and that silence had been fermenting in her all year, sour and stubborn. She wanted the words that would have been better than the silence. She didn't have them yet.

Then Elliana missed the next two Tuesdays. When she came back she took Mya into the hallway by the gym, past the trophy case, and stood with her arms crossed over her backpack straps. "Can I ask you something and you not be weird about it."

"You can ask."

"Dominic and I, we didn't, but it was close, and now I have this thing on my, whatever, and I want to get checked. But my mom would have to come, right? She'd have to sign something. She still checks my grades like I'm twelve." Elliana's voice was flat, rehearsed, the way people talk when they've practiced a sentence in the shower.

Mya opened her mouth to say probably, and then closed it, because she actually didn't know. She had been teaching this material for weeks and she had never once checked the part about clinics. That embarrassed her in a sharp, specific way, like discovering the word she'd been defining for others was spelled differently in the dictionary.

"I'll come with you," she said. "But let's just go and ask. Saturday."

The clinic on Fourth Street had a waiting room with a fish tank and a broken corner of ceiling tile, and a smell like hand sanitizer and old carpet. Mya sat beside Elliana and filled out nothing, holding her friend's jacket while Elliana gave her name to the receptionist in a voice pitched too high. When the nurse came out, a woman with gray in her ponytail and sneakers that squeaked, Elliana asked the question all in one breath: whether her mom had to sign, because she wasn't eighteen.

The nurse shook her head before the sentence was even finished. "All fifty states, plus Washington, DC, let minors consent to STI testing and treatment on their own," she said. "No parent signature. Some states do set a minimum age, so I'll double-check ours for you, but you're fine." She said it the way she'd clearly said it a thousand times, bored and kind at once, and Elliana's shoulders came down from around her ears like something unlatching.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Elliana sat on the concrete bumper of the last parking space and put her head in her hands, and Mya stood next to her not touching her, unsure whether touch was wanted, which after three weeks of a consent script felt like the one exam she hadn't studied for. "I've been scared for a month," Elliana said into her palms. "A month. And I could have just walked in."

At the Tuesday session Mya told Ms. Smith she wanted to change the lesson plan. "We teach the facts," Ms. Smith said, "and the facts are on the handout." Mya said the handout had never told Elliana anything, because Elliana had never been given a reason to trust a handout, and Ms. Smith looked at her for a long moment and then said the plan was hers to change.

So the following week Mya stood in front of fourteen juniors with her palms sweating through the notecards, and she skipped the smooth part. She told them about the clinic on Fourth Street, the fish tank, the nurse's squeaking shoes. She said the law out loud, all fifty states and DC, no parent signature, some states with a minimum age, and she watched a boy in the second row stop doodling. Then she got to the consent part, the part she'd rewritten four times, and she looked at the girl with the doodling boy's hand near her elbow, and she began, "Consent isn't a form you sign once. It's something you check on every single time."

"How do you check on it?" someone called from the back.

"You ask," Mya said. "Out loud. Even if it's awkward. Especially then."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Migration can reshape a pyramid: some Gulf states, such as Qatar, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there.
story:
Dylan spread the printed charts across the kitchen table while his mother browned onions at the stove. The assignment from Mr. Rivera was due Monday: pick two countries, read their population pyramids, and argue whether each would need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years. He had chosen France, whose pyramid narrowed to a point like a strained neck, and Qatar, whose shape made no sense at all.

"That one's wrong," he said, more to himself than to her. "Look at it. There's this huge bulge in the middle, and it's all on the male side. Nothing narrows. It looks like a wasp." He turned the paper sideways, then back. His mother leaned over his shoulder for a second and went back to her onions.

He opened his phone and typed the country and the words chart error into the search bar. Nothing useful came up, so he took a photo of the pyramid and sent it to the group chat with Axelle and Bentley. Bentley answered first: "the printer ate it probably." Axelle answered four minutes later: "not an error. my cousin worked in doha for two years. look it up."

Dylan remembered the day Mr. Rivera had first put a pyramid on the board, back in September. Rivera had said almost nothing that day; he had made them look at it in silence for a full minute before letting anyone speak, and Dylan had been bored until the shape began to organize itself, bars widening and narrowing like a report card for an entire country. He had not felt that way about anything else in geography. There was a maxim Rivera kept repeating, "the shape remembers," and Dylan had written it in the margin of his notebook without thinking about what it meant.

Now he searched for Qatar itself, not the chart. He found a page of photographs of construction sites in Doha, rows of men in matching coveralls waiting for buses at dawn, and then, further down, a line about foreign workers, and it assembled itself in his head at once. The bulge was not a birth rate. It was migration, workers who had arrived grown, mostly men, and the pyramid was simply recording them where they stood. The shape remembers, he thought. It remembers even the people who were never born there.

He typed this into the chat. Bentley replied, "wait so the chart isn't about the country's people at all?" and Dylan wrote back, "it's about whoever is standing in it." Axelle sent a voice message: "That's exactly it. Some Gulf states show that big bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there." He listened to it twice. It was strange, he thought, that a chart could be accurate and misleading at the same time, and he could not decide which it was.

He tried to build his argument for the essay. The obvious move was to say Qatar needed neither schools nor nursing homes, only more of whatever working-age men required, but that was too easy and probably wrong; the men would age somewhere, in a country that might not be Qatar, and that country's pyramid would carry the weight instead. He kept drafting and cutting sentences. His mother put a plate of rice and beans beside him and he ate without looking up.

At ten he called Axelle. "I think I have to write it as two different questions," he said. "What the country needs and what the chart shows. For France they're the same thing. For Qatar they're not." She said that sounded right but that she wasn't sure either, and that Rivera would probably give him extra credit for admitting it. He told her that admitting it felt like a dodge, and she said, "It's only a dodge if you stop there." He stayed on the phone with her while he retitled the document, and after he hung up he sat looking at the two pyramids side by side, the wasp and the narrowing neck, before he deleted his old opening line and typed a new one.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
Isla had claimed the table by the window in the public library because it had two things no other table offered: an outlet shaped so her charger actually fit, and a view of the parking lot where the mail truck turned in at four o'clock. She was sixteen, which meant that everyone who asked about college had the same follow-up, said in the tone reserved for dogs walking on their hind legs. She had applied anyway, one school, early, and the answer was due to arrive any day now, which was why she was spending her afternoon refreshing a portal that a librarian had gently suggested would not update faster under surveillance.

"You're staring at it like it's a microwave," said Tavin, dropping into the chair across from her with a stack of AP bio flashcards he had no intention of using. "It'll ding when it's done."

"Portals don't ding."

"Yours should. They should send it by owl. Like the British."

"That's a book, Tavin." She closed the laptop halfway, which she had read somewhere reduced strain on the hinge, and which made her feel, in an atavistic way, like she was protecting something small under a shell. The trouble was that she could not decide what she actually wanted the letter to say. Ms. Virtanen, the librarian, had asked her that directly last week while stamping returns: did she want yes, or did she want permission? Isla had said yes, obviously, but the word had come out too fast, the way answers do when they haven't been checked against the question.

Two tables over, a senior from her school sat with her mother at one of the library's ancient computers, the kind whose fans sounded like a small aircraft taking off. The screen glowed with a long form, and the mother kept leaning in and squinting. "It says list your income, not your dreams, Mom," the senior said. "This is the FAFSA. It's what you fill out to get federal financial aid. Pell Grants, federal loans, all of that." The mother said something about grants being free money, and the senior said yes, that was the general idea, and could they please finish tonight because the state deadline was tomorrow and the state used this same form to decide its own aid. The college did too, apparently, which was why one bad evening at a slow computer could cost them thousands.

Isla listened while pretending to study. She had assumed, in the vague way she assumed most things about money, that if she got in, the getting in would be the hard part, and everything after would arrange itself like iron filings around a magnet. Watching the senior hit the back button for the third time and mutter a word her mother pretended not to hear, she understood that the form was the second gate, and that nobody had mentioned it to her because nobody expected a sixteen-year-old to be standing at the first one yet.

"Your mom's going to have to do that," Tavin said, following her gaze. "For you. Next year."

"Next year, or, you know." She tapped the closed laptop. "If."

"If what?"

"Portal."

"Ah." He reshuffled his flashcards without looking at them. "My sister says waiting desensitizes you. Like cold water. By the time the answer comes, you feel nothing, you just open it."

"That's the saddest thing anyone's ever said to me at this table, and you once told me your bio grade at this table."

At four, the mail truck came and went, and the little post office annex in the library lobby got its delivery, and Isla did not go over there, because she had decided that checking in person was beneath her, a decision that lasted nine minutes. Ms. Virtanen was at the desk sorting the pigeonholes when Isla arrived, out of breath from a distance of forty feet.

"Nothing today for you," Ms. Virtanen said. "I checked."

"You checked?"

"I always check for the ones who circle the lobby like that. There's an epistemology to waiting, you know." Isla blinked, and Ms. Virtanen smiled. "How do you know what you know. Some people know from a screen. Some people need paper in the hand." She held up an envelope, thin and plain, business-size, with the college's return address in the corner. "This one arrived for a senior, actually. The one fighting with her mother over the form. Do you want to take it to her, or is that too much power for one person?"

Isla carried the envelope across the room like it might go off. The senior took it, looked at her mother, looked at the unfinished form on the screen, and put the envelope down flat under her hand without opening it. "After we submit this," she said. "I'm not reading anything until the state has my numbers. Priorities, Mom. Pell Grants before destiny."

Then she slit it open with a car key, and Isla, standing there, saw her whole face do something complicated and unresolved, and the senior looked up and said, "Well. Someone's going to have to fix that form, because apparently I'm going."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
The hardware store on Marsh Road had a bell above the door that rang twice for every customer, and by the end of his second week Benjamin could gauge the mood of the place by the sound. A quick double chime meant someone buying a single bolt; a slow, tired ring meant a project, a list, an afternoon. He had taken the job in March because his mother had stopped pretending the tuition letters were junk mail, and because Aayan had said the owner, Ms. Dela Cruz, paid fairly and never yelled. Both turned out to be true, which was more than Benjamin had expected from any adult-run institution.

He learned the aisles fast: the difference between a machine bolt and a carriage bolt, which sandpaper grit the carpenters wanted by feel rather than number, where the obsolescent drawer pulls lived in the back, kept for the old houses on Hill Street whose owners refused to update anything. Ms. Dela Cruz let him work the register alone after nine days. When he mentioned this at lunch, Sasha, who bagged groceries across town, said her manager still hovered after four months, and something about the comparison made the week feel earned.

Then came the week of the fence. A contractor named Voss bought out the cedar pickets and needed them delivered and stained, and Ms. Dela Cruz asked Benjamin if he could take on extra hours over the school break. He said yes before doing the arithmetic. By Thursday his hands were stiff with splinters and the heat had begun to enervate him, that specific drained heaviness where even lifting a water bottle felt like a negotiation. He worked Monday through Saturday, opened and closed twice, and clocked forty-seven hours. He did not count them. He only knew he was tired in a way school had never made him.

The paycheck came in a thin envelope on a Tuesday. Benjamin read it at the picnic table behind the store, and read it again. The bottom number was larger than he expected, and above it, printed in the plain font of a machine with no interest in his confusion, was a second rate, higher than his usual one, attached to seven of his hours. His first thought, embarrassingly, was that it was a mistake, and his second was that he should say nothing and hope nobody noticed. He sat with both thoughts for a while. The veneer of being an easygoing kid who didn't ask questions had served him well with teachers and coaches, but it had never been tested against money.

He asked Aayan first, since Aayan's older sister worked retail. "That's overtime," Aayan said, dunking a fry in ketchup with the calm of someone relaying family law. "Federal thing. Non-exempt employees get one and a half times their regular rate for hours past forty in a workweek." Benjamin asked what non-exempt meant and Aayan admitted his sister had called it "people like us," which was not a legal definition but did the job. Sasha leaned across the table. "Wait, I've worked over forty during holidays. Nobody switched my rate." She pulled out her phone and looked at her own pay stubs, three weeks of them, and her face changed.

They went back and forth the way they did about everything now, college essays, whether to room together, whether honesty was a virtue or a strategy. Sasha said her manager was decent, probably, just disorganized. Benjamin said that was exactly the kind of excuse he had been drafting in his own head for staying quiet, and it sounded worse out loud. What he could not resolve, even walking home, was whether the right move was to report it or to talk to the manager first, whether the law was a floor or a weapon, and he told them honestly that he did not know yet. Aayan said not knowing yet was allowed.

The next morning Benjamin brought his envelope to Ms. Dela Cruz, laid it flat on the counter between a display of tape measures and a jar of donation change. He said he had questions about the second rate and about how it worked, because a friend of his might not have gotten it. Ms. Dela Cruz looked at the stub, then at him, and did not seem insulted. She said the store's software computed it automatically and she had never had to explain it before, and then she said Sasha's manager could check the same way, quietly, without anyone being accused of anything.

Benjamin texted Sasha from the parking lot: talk to him first, ask him to look at the stubs, the rate is one and a half times regular past forty in a week. He stood a minute longer in the March cold, the bell over the door ringing twice behind him for a customer he would never see, and then he walked toward school with his hands in his pockets, the envelope folded once in his jacket, the ink still sharp enough to read through the paper.

She wrote back before he reached the corner: "He's looking at them right now."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The United States baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and its bulge on the pyramid has now moved into the retirement ages.
story:
The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Halvorsen had been specific: choose a country, analyse its population pyramid, and predict whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Jordan had chosen the United States more or less at random, printed the pyramid from the school library, and folded it into the pocket of the passenger door, where it stayed while his father drove the four hours to his grandparents' house for the weekend.

He was supposed to finish the essay on the drive. Instead he had written two sentences and then argued by text with Jaiveer, who had chosen Nigeria and claimed the answer there was obvious, more schools, no contest. "You're just reading the shape," Jordan typed back. "You have to say why." Jaiveer sent a photograph of his own pyramid with the wide base circled in red pen, and Jordan put the phone face down on his knee and watched the fields go by.

Laura called somewhere past the second gas station. She had the same class but a different position, that the whole assignment commodified people, turning them into bars on a chart so somebody could decide what to build and what to profit from. "A pyramid doesn't want anything," she said. "It's just a count. The wanting gets added later."

"That's the point of the assignment," Jordan said. "The count tells you what's coming."

"The count doesn't tell you what to do about it. You're acting like the chart makes the decision for you."

He told her he'd think about it and hung up, and then felt the small dishonesty of that, because he mostly wanted her to be wrong and couldn't yet say why.

At his grandparents' house the driveway was full of cars, some neighbours' reunion his grandmother had organized, and the kitchen was loud. His grandfather was in his belligerent mood, the one where every remark came out as an argument, telling a man by the sink that the county had closed the school two towns over and what did anyone expect, nobody young left to fill it. Jordan stood at the counter with a paper cup of punch and listened. There were a lot of grey heads in the room. He counted, without meaning to, the way he'd been counting all week.

He went out to the car for his jacket and took the folded pyramid with him, and sat on the trunk with it flattened against his knees. The chart for the United States had a bulge in the middle, a swelling band where the bars pushed outward, and he found the ages that went with it and did the arithmetic against his fingers. The bulge was people born between 1946 and 1964. He worked out his grandfather's birth year, 1951, and looked back at the chart, and then at the house, where through the window he could see his grandmother carrying a cake toward the long table, one of maybe forty people in that room born inside those years. His grandfather. Half the neighbours. The bulge wasn't an abstraction; it was this reunion, and it had already moved into the retirement ages on the chart, the whole swelling shifted up into the upper bands of the pyramid.

He had written in his draft, the two finished sentences, that the country would need more schools. Sitting on the trunk he crossed that out with a pen from his jacket. More nursing homes, or something like them, and fewer of the schools his grandfather was complaining about, and both things at once from the same shape. He texted Jaiveer: "You were right about yours but I had mine backwards." Then, after a minute, he texted Laura too, because it seemed dishonest not to. "The chart doesn't decide. But it's not nothing either. I'm still figuring out where the line is." She replied with a single question mark, then: "Bring it Monday, we'll fight about it at lunch."

Inside, they were singing now, badly, the whole kitchen of them. His grandfather's voice came through the wall louder than the rest, off-key and refusing to quit. Jordan folded the pyramid along its old creases and went back in to get a second piece of cake before it ran out.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
story:
Jason arrived at the counter of the coffee shop at four, ordered a medium drip, and took the corner table where the outlets worked. He spread out his logic notes, two debate briefs, and a photocopied page of practice problems, and began to collate them into one stack he could actually study from. The unit test was Monday, and Mr. Reddy had a habit of putting validity questions on it, the kind where you had to say whether an argument held together regardless of whether it was true.

Ulysse came in ten minutes later, shaking rain off his jacket, and dropped into the chair across from Jason without ordering anything. He leaned over the practice sheet. "Number four again?"

"Number four," Jason said. "If the tide pool is littoral, then the crabs migrate. The tide pool is littoral. Therefore the crabs migrate." It was from a worksheet Mr. Reddy had built out of marine science vocabulary, apparently to prove a point Jason hadn't yet grasped.

"None of that means anything to me," Ulysse said. He took the pen out of Jason's hand, crossed out the words, and wrote above them: If the flim is zorped, then the blug runs. The flim is zorped. Therefore the blug runs. "There. Same problem."

Jason looked at it and felt something shift, the way a lock feels when it turns. The argument was garbage, every word of it invented, and still it worked. You had to accept the conclusion if you accepted the two lines above it. He said so, slowly, testing it. "If P then Q. P. Therefore Q. It doesn't matter what P and Q are. It could be crabs, it could be flims, it could be anything."

"That's modus ponens," said Karissa, who had come up behind them with a chai and now pulled over the third chair. "Mr. Reddy said the name about six times on Tuesday. You were drawing in your notebook."

"I was drawing the tide pool," Jason said, but he wrote the words down anyway, and underlined them. The form was the thing. That was the whole point of the unit, and for the first time he could see it as a shape independent of its contents, a container you could pour anything into, even nonsense, and it still wouldn't leak.

Karissa tapped the debate brief on top of his stack. "Then explain your affirmative case to me, since you're so smart now."

He read the opening line of it aloud: If the school funds the ferry program, then island students will attend at higher rates. The school will fund the ferry program. Therefore island students will attend at higher rates. It was the same skeleton. He recognized it the way you recognize a face in a stranger's crowd. But the difference nagged at him. "Except in the debate, the first line is a prediction, not a definition. I can't actually verify it the way I can verify that the flim is zorped."

"So it's still modus ponens," Ulysse said, "just with a shakier P."

"That's the problem, though. Formally valid, probably unsound." Jason pulled the brief toward himself and crossed out the second line, wrote the school will not fund the ferry program above it, and stared at what remained. If the conditional held and the funding failed, the conclusion didn't follow. He couldn't derive what the attendance would do. There was a version of the case where he argued the conditional itself, and a version where he argued the funding, and he had been treating them as one argument when they were two.

Karissa watched him work. "You're overcomplicating. You're a pragmatist, just argue the one the judges will buy."

"Maybe. But if the conditional is wrong, the whole case is a zorped flim." He said it to be funny, but as he said it, he understood that it wasn't quite right either. The nonsense argument had been perfectly sound within its own world; his case might be perfectly broken within this one, and formal validity couldn't tell him which. That part, the part where the form was silent, was the part Mr. Reddy's test couldn't grade and his debate round couldn't resolve.

Mr. Reddy himself came through the door at that moment, oversized umbrella under his arm, and stopped at their table on his way to the counter. He glanced at the practice sheet, at the crossed-out crabs and the nonsense words, and raised an eyebrow at Jason.

"Monday," Mr. Reddy said. "Number four?"

Jason covered the sheet with his hand. "I'm ready for number four. It's everything after number four I'm still deciding about."

Mr. Reddy ordered his coffee and sat down two tables away with the crossword. Jason slid the debate brief across to Karissa. "Pick one," he said. "You're the judge. Which P do I fight for?"

Karissa put her chai down and put her finger on the conditional.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
Olivier set his laptop on his grandfather's kitchen table because it was the only table in the house that didn't wobble, and because his grandfather, who could no longer hear well enough for television, liked having someone else in the room. The assignment was due Sunday night: build a class called Book in Java, with private fields, getter methods, and a constructor that works, then test all of it. Mr. Bélanger had written the requirements on the board in his cramped, forward-leaning hand, and had said only, "Test what you build, not what you hope you built."

The house smelled of his grandfather's coffee, boiled too long, a smell Olivier had hated as a child and now associated with getting things done. He opened the file and began typing. He wrote the class shell first, then the fields: private String title, private String author, private int pages. He remembered Mr. Bélanger saying that private meant the outside world had to knock politely, through getter methods, rather than reaching in. That part made a kind of sense to Olivier, the way his grandfather's toolshed made sense: everything in its place, nothing borrowed without asking.

The trouble started at the constructor. Olivier knew roughly what it was for, a method that ran when the object was created, filling in the fields. He typed it the way he typed every other method, out of habit rather than decision. His fingers produced "public void Book(String t, String a, int p)" and then the assignments, title equals t, author equals a, pages equals p. It looked correct to him. It looked, if anything, tidy.

In the test class he wrote a main method, created a Book, and printed the result of calling getTitle. The console showed null. He created another one, printed getAuthor, and got null again, and then a third time, because some part of him believed that repetition could portend a different outcome, that the machine might relent. It did not relent. The fields stayed empty, the getters returned nothing, and the sun moved across the kitchen table without changing anything.

He texted Isaac, who was further ahead in the unit. "my constructor won't run," he wrote, and pasted the line of code. Then he texted Hamza, who was behind but who read everything twice and caught things other people skimmed past. While he waited, his grandfather shuffled in, looked at the screen with its wall of small grey letters, and asked what it was supposed to be. "A program," Olivier said. "It's supposed to remember a book." His grandfather nodded slowly, as though this were a reasonable thing for a program to do, and sat down across from him with his coffee.

Hamza replied first. He sent back the pasted line with one word circled, or the texting equivalent of circled, which was an arrow and three exclamation points, all pointed at the word void. Olivier stared at it. He had written void in front of a hundred methods by now; void was what you wrote when a method gave nothing back. But Isaac's message arrived a minute later and said it plainly: "A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void." Olivier read the sentence twice, deleted the word, and ran the test.

This time the console printed the title, the author, the page count. It was such a small thing, four letters removed, and it had cost him most of an afternoon. He sat back and thought about how the compiler had never complained, had accepted void Book as some ordinary method that happened to share a name with the class, a method no one ever called, sitting there like a door that opened onto wallpaper. There was something almost pernicious about it, an error that made no noise, that let you believe you had built something when you had only described it. Isaac, who believed every rule should be memorised before you were allowed near a keyboard, would call Olivier's trial-and-error method an indictment of how he studied. Hamza, who believed rules only stuck after you'd been wounded by them once, would say this was the only way anyone learned anything. Olivier suspected the truth was uglier and sat somewhere between the two, though he couldn't have said where, exactly.

He wrote two more tests anyway, even though the assignment technically required only one, because Mr. Bélanger's sentence had come back to him. He tested that the pages field returned the right number, then that a second Book object kept its own title separate from the first. Both passed. He still didn't fully understand why the constructor's shape mattered so much, only that it did, and that he would notice the word void the next time, the way you notice a stair that once gave way under you.

He showed his grandfather the screen, the green line that said the tests had passed, expecting the old man to squint and nod politely. Instead his grandfather leaned in, tapped the glass with one crooked finger, right on the passing test, and said, "So that's the one that remembers the book." Then, before Olivier could explain that all of it was the program, his grandfather added, "Good. Write one next that remembers where I put my glasses."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
The driveway was long enough for maybe four cars parked nose to tail, and Samantha had spent a week measuring it in her head, pacing it out after dark while her mother watched from the porch and pretended not to. Mr. Zhu, the neighbour two houses down who taught piano and, apparently, driving, sat in the passenger seat of his old sedan with his hands folded in his lap like a man waiting for a recital to begin. Samantha adjusted the mirror for the third time. Behind the chain-link fence, Lauralie sat cross-legged on her own driveway with a sketchpad, ostensibly drawing the mailboxes, actually waiting to witness whatever happened, because Lauralie's summer want was simple and enormous: to be the person who saw everything first and reported it.

"Whenever you're ready," Mr. Zhu said. "Foot on the brake, then start it."

She started it. The engine transfixxed her for a second, the whole car shivering alive under her hands, and she almost laughed at how small the movement of her foot had to be to make so much happen. She released the brake the way her mother had described, feather-light, and the car rolled forward two feet and stopped, and it felt like a beginning.

"Not yet," Mr. Zhu said, mild as weather. "Seat belt first. Every time. Even here."

"It's the driveway."

"Especially here. Habits don't know the difference between a driveway and a highway. That's the whole trouble with habits, and also their whole value." He said it without lecturing, the way he said most things, and while she pulled the belt across her chest he added nothing further, which she understood was itself a kind of teaching.

She buckled it, then, because she was sixteen and could not let a rule stand on authority alone, she took out her phone. Lauralie wandered over and leaned on the fence to read over her shoulder. According to the CDC, Samantha found, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. She read it twice. Half. Not some vague fraction, not a scolding, just half, and she sat with the strangeness of that, the way a number could be both small and enormous at once. Lauralie, who had failed her own learner's permit test in June for reasons she refused to disclose, said, "Half of what, though. Half of dying. That's a weird thing to cut in half."

"It's not a promise," Samantha said slowly. "It's more like a taxonomy of what usually happens. Most people who get hurt weren't belted, so the belt moves you into the other group." She was assembling it as she spoke, the two ideas she'd been carrying all week: her mother's version, where rules were walls you didn't question, and her own, where a rule was only worth following if you could see what it was standing on. The CDC number was the footing. She still didn't like being told. But she could follow a thing she understood, and she could admit, privately, that the difference between those two kinds of obedience was smaller than she wanted it to be.

"Are we philosophizing," Lauralie said, "or are you going to drive before the streetlights come on?"

Mr. Zhu was watching the fence line with an expression Samantha couldn't parse, and then she could: Lauralie wanted a turn. She had failed the test and told no one the real reason and had been insouciant about the whole business, shrugging it off at the pool, at the diner, everywhere, and now she was standing at a fence watching someone else do the thing she couldn't. Samantha unbuckled, opened the door, and waved her over. "Ride along. Ask him about the written part. He's a teacher, it's pathological."

Mr. Zhu smiled at that. Lauralie climbed into the back, and Samantha pulled the belt across her chest again, and this time the click of it sounded like a small decision rather than a command obeyed. She let her foot off the brake. The car rolled to the end of the driveway and stopped, crooked, well short of the sidewalk, and nobody said anything about the crookedness, which she would remember later.

"Again," Mr. Zhu said. "From the top."

She reached for the keys, and Lauralie leaned forward between the seats and said, "Wait. Before you go. Did you know that seat belts cut serious injuries in half?"

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
story:
The register at Danforth's Hardware had been slow since four, which gave Sarah time to prop her econ notebook against the racks of WD-40 and stare at the essay prompt Mr. Nkosi had assigned. "Explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation." Her first draft was three sentences long and all of them were definitions she had copied from the textbook, the kind of writing that said nothing twice.

Bilal came back from the lumber aisle with a dolly and leaned on the counter. "Still that essay?"

"It's due Tuesday and I don't actually get it," Sarah said. "Like I can memorize the words, but if someone asked me why it works, I'd just repeat the words louder."

"So explain it to me," Bilal said. "Rylie said that's what you're supposed to do. Explain it to someone who doesn't know anything."

Sarah closed the notebook. "Okay. So the central bank raises interest rates, and that makes borrowing more expensive, so people buy less, and prices stop climbing so fast."

"And why do prices stop climbing?"

"Because demand falls."

"And why does falling demand slow inflation?"

She opened her mouth, then closed it. The words were stacked on each other like the paint cans in aisle six, each one resting on the one below, and when she pulled the bottom one out the whole tower wobbled. "I don't know what's underneath," she admitted. "I know the sequence but not the reason. And then there's this whole other part about the Fed wanting inflation at two percent, which makes no sense to me, because isn't any inflation bad? Why would two percent be success?"

Bilal shrugged. "You're asking the wrong guy. I failed that unit."

At closing time Sarah sat on an overturned crate by the paint mixer and searched on her phone. Most of what she found was either too simple or too dense, but one Fed page had a date, and she stopped on it the way you stop on a name you should have known. On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve had adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index. She read it twice, then a third time, because it didn't say two percent was ideal, or natural, or discovered like a law of physics. It said adopted. Chosen. A committee had sat in a room and picked a number, and that number, ever since, was the definition of doing the job right.

"It's a decision," she said out loud to the empty store. "Not a fact. A decision."

The manager poked his head out of the back office and told her to lock up, so she locked up, but on the walk home she kept turning it over. She had been treating the two percent the way her grandmother treated scripture, something to valorize rather than question, and the essay had broken under the weight of it. If the target was chosen, then everything downstream of it was chosen too. Raising rates wasn't a correction of some natural error; it was a lever pulled to steer toward a number people had agreed on. And a lever pulled meant an apportionment of cost, she realized, walking past the darkened bakery. When borrowing got expensive, somebody's loan got rejected. Somebody's expansion didn't happen. The economy cooled, and "the economy" wasn't a cloud, it was the bakery, and Mr. Okafor two doors down who had been trying to refinance since spring.

Tuesday morning she read the essay to Rylie before class. "It's good," Rylie said, "but the last paragraph is weird. You basically say you don't know if two percent is the right number."

"I don't. Nobody in the essay knows. The Fed chose it and everyone's worked backward from there ever since. I can explain the mechanism now, the whole chain from rates to borrowing to demand to prices, I made Bilal sit through it twice at work. But whether two percent is right, or just familiar, that part I can't get to."

"That's going to cost you the grade."

"Probably."

Rylie looked at her like she had decided to wear mismatched shoes on purpose. "Then why keep it?"

Sarah thought about the belligerent tone of her own first draft, all that false certainty, definitions marching in a line. "Because the other version was a lie I could have gotten an A on."

In class, Mr. Nkosi returned the essays two days later, and when he reached Sarah's he paused a moment before setting it face-down on her desk, which was something he did only when he wanted to talk after. She turned it over. A B, and in the margin, circled twice, the date January 25, 2012, and beside it: "Come see me about this."

She sat through the rest of the period with the paper in her lap, deciding. After the bell she was still deciding, and then she was standing at his door, and then she knocked.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Borrowing $300,000 for 30 years at a fixed 6 percent rate means paying more than $347,000 in interest, more than the amount borrowed.
story:
Carter had been to Francisco's apartment maybe forty times, but he had never noticed the envelope on the fridge until the day it had FINAL NOTICE stamped across it in red. He was standing at the counter making peanut butter toast while Francisco searched for his controller, and the envelope kept catching his eye the way a loose tooth did, something wrong that you couldn't stop probing. The kitchen smelled like the toast and like the lemon cleaner Francisco's mom used on Fridays, and through the window came the sound of the neighbor's dog losing its mind at a pigeon, again.

"Is your mom selling?" Carter asked, because Francisco had said something about it last week, offhand, while they were arguing about whether Keagan's new haircut was bombastic or just confident. Francisco had said "we might be moving" the way you say you might skip a party, like it barely mattered. It clearly mattered now.

"Rent's going up three hundred," Francisco said from inside the closet. "Landlord wants more because the building's near the new station. Mom's talking about buying instead, but the places she's looking at want a down payment, like twenty percent, and she has, I don't know, some money saved, but not that." He emerged, controller in hand, hair flattened on one side. "And you have to give them a deposit when you rent somewhere too, first and last month. She did that here. Four years ago. It was a whole thing."

Carter buttered his toast. He knew about deposits the way he knew about most money things, vaguely, the way he knew the bus schedule, something adults handled. But three hundred more a month was thirty-six hundred a year, and he could do that math fast because it felt like something he should be able to hold onto.

Later that afternoon, after Francisco destroyed him twice at the fighting game and Keagan arrived with a bag of day-old donuts from his shift, they ended up on Francisco's bed with the laptop, ostensibly for homework. Instead Francisco pulled up a listing for a small house on Marsh Street, the kind with a porch and a yard the size of a picnic blanket. "Mom keeps looking at this one," he said. "It's three hundred thousand. Which is insane, but she says renting is just throwing money away, her words, and I don't even know what that means."

Carter opened a mortgage calculator because he wanted to see the monthly number, something he could compare against three hundred more in rent, apples against apples. He typed in three hundred thousand, thirty years, six percent, fixed, because the site had a little dropdown and that was the default and Francisco said that's what his mom's bank guy had quoted. The monthly payment came up and it was high but not impossible, and Carter was about to close the tab when he saw the other line, the one underneath, labeled total interest.

His first thought was that the site was broken. He refreshed it. Same number. Borrowing three hundred thousand for thirty years at six percent fixed meant paying more than three hundred forty-seven thousand in interest, more than the amount borrowed. More. You'd hand the bank more money than they ever handed you. He turned the laptop so Keagan could see, and Keagan leaned in, chew off a piece of donut, and said, "That can't be right, run it again," so Carter ran it again, slower, like the number might behave differently if he watched it appear.

"So renting isn't throwing money away," Francisco said slowly. "It's just paying for a place without the extra three hundred forty-seven thousand attached." But then he frowned, because he was remembering, Carter could tell, the time in seventh grade when his mom had been late on the rent and the landlord's letters had come, and how he'd carried that fear around like a coin in his pocket all year. "Except the landlord can raise it whenever. And you never own anything at the end. You don't get the house."

"Maybe the interest is a disincentive," Keagan said, spraying donut crumbs, "so you don't borrow money you can't pay back," and Carter said he didn't think banks were trying to discourage anyone, which started an argument that lasted through two more donuts and got loud enough that Francisco's mom banged on the wall from the next room, even though she wasn't home yet and it was actually the upstairs neighbor, which cracked them up for a full minute.

The thing that had destabilized Carter wasn't the number itself, he decided, walking home under the streetlights with frosting smell still on his hands. It was that Francisco's mom had probably already seen that same total interest line, sitting alone at this same kitchen table, and had decided something anyway, or was still deciding, and Carter had no idea which. Renting, owning, either way you paid and paid and the difference was some shape you couldn't see until the end, thirty years out, longer than Carter had been alive.

His phone buzzed. It was Francisco: "twist. mom just called. the marsh st house is under agreement. somebody bought it in cash." Carter stood on the corner for a second, then typed back, "somebody had 300 thousand just lying around?" The three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again. "she says the guy next door. retired plumber. never rented a day in his life."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The booth at Marconi's had been pushed together for nine people, and Mason ended up wedged between his uncle and Scarlett, with Kenley across the table and Ms. Tang, his old chemistry teacher, at the end with a plate of calamari she kept passing down to whoever looked underfed. On the big screen above the bar, the semifinal was tied in the seventy-first minute. Mason had played center back for four years of club soccer, and his uncle had watched even longer, which was the problem, because the two of them had been litigating the ref's decisions since the opening whistle.

His uncle did most of the litigating. He leaned forward at every whistle, hands spread, addressing the table as though it were a panel of judges. When the opposing winger collected a pass two steps behind the last defender and buried it in the net, the uncle was on his feet before the celebration finished.

"Offside! Look at him, he's miles off! That's the third time the linesman's missed it tonight."

The replay held on the scorer, alone near the six-yard box. Mason felt something assemble itself in his mind, the way a mechanism does when you finally have all the parts. "Wait," he said. "The ball came from the corner kick. There's no offside from a corner." His uncle scoffed, and Kenley, who had never watched a soccer match in her life, looked from one to the other like a spectator at a different sport. Mason pushed on, slower now, testing each step. "And being in an offside position isn't an offence by itself. You only get penalized if you're involved in active play. And you can't be offside from a throw-in, a goal kick, or a corner either."

"That's not how it works," his uncle said, but with less certainty, and he took a long drink of his beer while the announcers confirmed the goal. Mason didn't press. He'd learned from years of car rides that winning the argument in the first minute usually cost him the next hour, so he passed the calamari down to his cousin, who had been eyeing it without wanting to ask.

The minutes wound toward full time, the light outside the restaurant windows going crepuscular, headlights bleeding gold across the parking lot. When the attacking team won a throw-in deep in the corner, Mason found himself leaning forward, his own knowledge suddenly interesting to him, the rules no longer things he'd memorized for a badge test but a lens. He had spent his whole playing life trying to be disciplined, to hold the line, to avoid precisely the positions that gave attackers their advantage, and it had never once occurred to him that the rule itself was generous, full of exemptions and second chances. He'd been playing a harsher game than the one on the field.

Scarlett watched him more than the screen after that. She had known Mason since sophomore year, when he'd corrected a substitute teacher's chemistry problem and then apologized for a full minute, and she recognized the particular stillness he got when he was turning something over. She also noticed his uncle drawing breath for another complaint and, before it could land, slid the breadbasket in front of him, which bought everyone ninety seconds of chewing. When the winger again stood in an offside position, clearly beyond the last defender, and the crowd groaned in anticipation, Scarlett saw Mason open his mouth and close it again. The winger stayed where he was, taking no part, and the referee waved play on.

"He's not doing anything," the uncle said, half a question.

"He's offside if he gets involved," Mason said. "Not just for standing there."

His uncle nodded slowly, and something in his posture loosened, the litigiousness draining out of him for the first time all night. Ms. Tang raised her glass a few inches, not quite a toast, and Kenley said, "So the whole rule is just, like, a thing you can argue about forever?" and Mason said, "Pretty much," and Scarlett laughed into her napkin.

In the eighty-ninth minute the ball came out to the winger, who had drifted back onside, and he crossed it low, and the striker arrived at the near post. The restaurant erupted. His uncle threw both arms around Mason's shoulders and shook him, and the waitress appeared with a tray of waters nobody had ordered, setting them down along the table for whoever needed them. On the screen the players sprinted toward the corner flag, and Mason stood up without quite deciding to, one hand raised toward the screen, still holding his uncle's wrist.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Quran, in Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, exempts people who are ill or travelling from fasting during Ramadan, directing them to make up the same number of days later.
story:
The cultural festival had taken over the school gym on a Saturday in March, and Jesse had agreed to run the interfaith booth mostly because Sofie said he owed her for the chemistry disaster of February. The plan was simple: pamphlets, a poster about fasting traditions across religions, a bowl of dates, and a folding table that wobbled no matter how he shimmed it. What he had not planned on was Kolby arriving at noon with a printout of the debate topic for their ethics class, slapping it down between the dates and the Buddhist pamphlets, and saying, "Settle this for me."

The topic was whether ancient religious rules still bind people in modern life, and Kolby had decided to make it personal. "My cousin's fasting this month, right, Ramadan, but she's got a basketball tournament three provinces away and she says it's fine to skip the fast, and my mom says that's just making it convenient." Kolby leaned on the table until it wobbled again. "Mr. Ahmadi says we can't argue it without the actual text. So get the actual text."

Jesse's own problem was quieter but the same shape. His uncle was flying in from Karachi during Ramadan, and Jesse, who had fasted with his family since he was twelve, had a provincial debate finals trip that would put him on a bus for nine hours on two of the fasting days. He had been planning to just power through, because powering through felt like the point. He found the verse on his phone while Kolby watched, and read it under his breath: Surah 2, Al-Baqarah. People who are ill or travelling are exempted from fasting during Ramadan, and directed to make up the same number of days later. He read it twice, and the second time something loosened in his chest, though he wasn't sure yet whether it was relief or the suspicion of relief.

"So it's allowed," Kolby said, reaching for a date. "Case closed."

It wasn't case closed, and Jesse surprised himself by saying so. Mr. Ahmadi was at the festival somewhere, drifting between booths in his grey cardigan, and Jesse went to find him, not to be taught but to have someone check his reasoning. He found him sampling the lentil soup at the Pakistani table. "I read Al-Baqarah," Jesse said. "Travellers and sick people are exempt. They make up the days later, same number." Mr. Ahmadi nodded and said only, "So what's your question?" and Jesse heard himself articulate the thing he'd been circling: the exemption is in the text itself, so following it isn't loosening the rule, it's following it more precisely. But then his uncle fasted through a work trip every year, on purpose, out of a devotion Jesse admired and didn't fully understand. Two readings of the same verse, both honest, and Jesse couldn't dismiss either one.

Back at the booth, the afternoon crowd thickened. A woman in a green headscarf stopped to argue, amiably but firmly, that people treat the traveller exemption like a loophole, that a polity doesn't hold together if everyone decides for themselves which commands are still binding. Jesse had the word abrogate in his head from a class discussion, the formal term for one ruling superseding another, and he used it carefully: the exemption doesn't abrogate the fast, it shapes it, the way a riverbank doesn't cancel the river. The woman tilted her head, considering, and said, "That's better reasoning than most adults give me at this table." Kolby, behind the dates, mouthed show-off.

Jesse's uncle texted him while the booth was at its busiest, and Jesse read the message with the noise of the festival washing around him. "I hear you are travelling for your debating in Ramadan. Your grandmother fasted through the partition year, through worse than a bus. But she also fed travellers who did not fast and never once scolded them. Read Al-Baqarah again and decide like a man, not like a boy who wants permission. Then tell me what you decided and why." Jesse read it three times. It was the first time his uncle had written to him as if his reasoning itself mattered, and it made the question heavier and lighter at once.

He wrote back before the festival wound down, sitting on the floor behind the booth with the fluorescent light buzzing above him. He kept it short.
