"I'll fast the days I can and make up the two travel days after, same number, like the verse says. Not because it's easier. Because I read the rule and the rule itself makes room for the road. And maybe on the bus I'll think about why the room is there. I'll tell you what I find." He pressed send, and his thumb stayed on the screen a second longer than it needed to.

When he stood up, Sofie was holding the last date out to him, and beyond her Kolby was photographing the poster for his cousin. "So what's the verdict?" Sofie asked. Jesse took the date, turned it over once in his fingers, and said, "Ask me after the trip."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech.
story:
The marble steps of city hall were still cold at noon, and Ashton climbed them two at a time with his binder pressed against his chest so the wind could not get at his note cards. Inside, the rotunda smelled of floor wax and old paper. A woman at the security desk pointed him toward the council chamber, where folding tables had been arranged to look like a courtroom, and where Julia was already taping a hand-lettered sign to the front of the judges' bench: MOCK COURT, CITY HALL SESSION, 2 PM.

"You're arguing both sides?" she asked, not looking up from the tape. "That's what Campbell told me. Petitioner and respondent, back to back."

"That's the assignment," Ashton said. "He says if you can't argue the side you hate, you don't understand the case."

The case involved a student suspended for a speech delivered off campus, outside school hours, that the school claimed was disruptive. Ashton had spent two weeks reading appeals and doctrines until his eyes ached, and the further he read the more the reading seemed to fold back on itself, each precedent qualifying another. He set his binder on the counsel table and flipped to the first page, where he had copied the amendment out by hand because typing it had felt too easy to forget.

Nikhil arrived with two coffees and the folded schedule. "They moved us," he said. "We're in the alderman's room instead, smaller, and the judges are Campbell plus two lawyers from the firm downtown." He paused, handing Ashton a coffee. "Also, the amendment. You want me to read it for your opening, or are you doing that thing where you recite it from memory?"

"Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech," Ashton said. "Ratified in 1791. First Amendment."

"Show-off," Nikhil said, but he smiled, and Ashton understood the smile as permission.

It had not always been permission. In the fall, before any of this, Ashton had stood in Campbell's classroom after the bell and insisted that free speech was simple, that words either cost something or they didn't. Campbell had leaned against his desk and said, "Then tomorrow, argue the other side, and see if it's still simple." Ashton had prevaricated, offering excuses about workload, and Campbell had watched him do it without comment, which was somehow worse than being corrected. That night Ashton stayed up until one in the morning building the case for the school's side, expecting to fail, and instead found that the failure never came. The argument assembled itself, coherent and even persuasive, and its coherence frightened him more than losing would have.

Now, in the alderman's room, the folding chairs filled. Campbell sat in the middle, flanked by the two lawyers, one of whom kept a fountain pen and turned it over in her fingers like a connoisseur of courtroom ceremony. Julia took her seat in the gallery beside a man Ashton recognized as the suspended student's father, his coat still buttoned, his hands folded as though he had been waiting a long time.

Ashton rose for the petitioner. He argued that the school's authority ended at the schoolhouse gate, that the suspension was a deleterious overreach, chilling exactly the speech the country had decided in 1791 it would not let Congress touch, and that a principal, like Congress, should make no law abridging the freedom of speech. The lawyers nodded at intervals. One of them asked about a case Ashton had not read, and he said so plainly, and the room seemed to settle rather than tighten.

Then he turned, physically, took two steps to the other lectern, and argued the school's side: that words spoken by a student still travel through the school the next morning, that disruption is not a metaphor but a hallway of fourteen-year-olds who could not do their work. He felt the father's stillness in the gallery behind him, felt it like a hand on the back of his neck, and understood that subtext was not something in books. It was a man in a buttoned coat listening to a boy explain, carefully and well, why his son's punishment might have been right.

At the recess, the father caught him by the water fountain. "You believe what you said up there?" the man asked. "The second part."

Ashton let the water run for a second before he turned it off. "I believe the words you can argue aren't always the words you believe," he said. "And I believe both sides are stronger than I want them to be. If you're asking whether I know the answer, I don't."

The man studied him, then nodded once, slowly, and went back into the room without another word. Julia appeared at Ashton's elbow with his binder, opened to a blank page. "Campbell wants closing statements," she said, "and you look like a man who hasn't written one."

He hadn't. He took the pen she offered and stood at the window, where below them the plaza was filling with an afternoon protest he had not known was scheduled, cardboard signs bobbing, a bullhorn crackling to life. He wrote his first line, crossed it out, and wrote it again, the amendment running through his head while the crowd below, small and certain, began to chant.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The guitar had belonged to Isaac's grandfather, and it came to the band room in a canvas case that smelled of dust and old adhesive. Mr. Rodríguez had said he could leave it behind the percussion cabinet, next to the marimba no one played, as long as he understood the cabinet stayed locked after four. Isaac had said he understood. That was a Tuesday.

By Thursday he had learned three chords from a video on his phone, but the chords sounded wrong, softened somehow, like speech through a wall. He turned the tuning pegs a little at a time and it got worse. Kadence, who had been copying timpani parts at the long table, came over and plucked the fattest string.

"That's not an E," she said. "It's way flat."

"I don't know what it's supposed to be," Isaac said. This was true. The video had shown him where to put his fingers but had assumed, without saying so, that the instrument was already in tune, and his grandfather, in the years before the guitar was given away, had not kept it that way.

Kadence went to the cabinet where the school kept its tuners and came back with a small black box the size of a candy bar. She clipped it to the headstock. "It reads the vibration," she said, and plucked the fattest string again. The needle sagged left of center. "So you're at D something. You need E."

He tightened the peg slowly, the way the video had shown him for other purposes, and the needle climbed. When it settled at E, the string rang out clearer than anything he had produced in two days. He wrote E on his hand in pen.

Malaya arrived for jazz ensemble early, the way she always did, and stood listening while he worked through the rest. She had played violin since she was six and she watched his hands with an interest he found faintly unnerving. "It goes in fourths," she said at one point, when he moved from the fat E string up to the next one. "On violin, all the strings are a fifth apart. You get used to that."

"What's a fourth?"

She hummed the first notes of a song Isaac half recognized, then said, "Not exactly. Here, watch the tuner." He plucked the second string and the needle said B flat, or something near it, and he tightened until it said A. He wrote A under the E. The third string wanted D. The fourth wanted G.

On the fifth string the tuner told him nothing helpful at first because he had plucked the wrong one, and Malaya laughed at him without apology. When he found the right string, tightened it, and watched the needle find B, she said, "There. That's the one that breaks the pattern. Everything else is a fourth, but that one's a third. It's why guitarists get lost going from G to B."

"Lost how?"

"Your hand expects the same distance and it isn't the same distance." She demonstrated by holding an imaginary neck and shifting her fingers a false interval. Isaac had no idea whether she was right about the distances, only that the tuner confirmed the letters, and he wrote them on his hand in order: E, A, D, G, B. Then the last string, thin as fishing line, and when he tightened it the needle arrived at E again. Two E's, an octave apart, though Malaya had to tell him the word for that too.

He played the three chords he knew and they sounded, for the first time, like the video. He played them again. Kadence had gone back to her timpani parts, but her foot was keeping time, which he chose to take as evidence.

The problem was that he had tuned the guitar by machine, and the machine told him the strings but not the logic. Malaya's talk of fourths and thirds was one way of thinking about it, the tuner's needle was another, and he could not yet tell whether they were the same knowledge wearing different clothes or two different things that happened to agree. That evening, at home, he retuned every string by ear against the E he remembered, got most of the way, checked himself against a phone app, and found he had drifted. He drifted less the next night. The night after that, less again. His left fingertips had gone tender, then callused, a small hardening that had incapacitated nothing and changed everything about how the strings felt.

By the following Tuesday he could tune the whole instrument from the low E upward without the box, and when Mr. Rodríguez passed through the band room after school and heard him playing, he stopped, listened to half a verse, and said nothing at all, which Isaac understood to be its own kind of grade.

He was thinking about his grandfather, who had played this same instrument at this same tension, or nearly, and about how the letters on his hand had washed off in the shower while the order stayed in his fingers. Kadance came over while he was packing up.

"Still got it in tune?"

"Check," Isaac said, and handed her the tuner.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
On the third day of the canoeing instructor course, Mackenzie got assigned to critique her partner's rescue demonstration, and her partner was Mael, who had once carried her backpack a mile when she'd twisted her ankle, and who was currently standing waist-deep in the lake with a sullen look, waiting. The demonstration had been bad. He'd rushed the approach, clipped the tow line wrong, and let the "victim" drift forty feet before noticing. Kelvin, lounging on the dock with his clipboard, raised an eyebrow at her.

"You're the evaluator," he said. "Evaluate."

"Mael was great," she called out. "Really solid."

Mael climbed out of the water and wrung his shirt without looking at her. That evening at the campfire he sat with his back to her, and Kelvin passed her a look across the flames like a note in class. She had lied to spare a friend, and the lie had landed as a dismissal, which was the opposite of what she'd intended, and she lay awake in her bunk composing apologies that all sounded like more lying.

The next morning she found Ms. Papadopoulos's resource binder on the porch of the boathouse, left open after the workshop on peer feedback. She flipped through it while waiting for the coffee water to boil. One page, photocopied crooked, described I-messages, statements that began with your own experience instead of an accusation, things like "I felt stuck when the slides came in late." A note in the margin said they'd been promoted by a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, back in the 1960s, as a way to raise a problem without blaming anybody. Mackenzie read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed almost too simple, like being told the cure for hiccups was a spoonful of sugar.

She practised on Kelvin first, because Kelvin could absorb anything. "Okay," she said, "turn this into one. 'You hog the good paddle every morning.'"

"Tell me how it feels, not what I did," Kelvin said, chewing a piece of toast. "Also, I do hog the good paddle. It has superior phenotype. Look at it. It's a beautiful paddle."

"That's not what phenotype means."

"It's gorgeous is what I'm saying. Come on, your turn."

She tried it out loud. "I start every morning off balance because I never know which paddle I'll get." Kelvin considered this, then nodded, and she felt something click into place, two ways of thinking she'd been holding apart, kindness and honesty, as if she'd had to choose, when all along they could be built into the same sentence. Though she was honest with herself about what stayed uncertain: whether it would work on someone whose feelings were already bruised, and whether she'd have the nerve to try.

She found Mael at the canoe rack, sorting lines. He started to prevaricate immediately, saying he'd been tired, that the water was choppy, that Kelvin's timing had thrown him off, and she let him run out of words.

"I went to give you feedback yesterday and I blew it," she said. "Here's what I actually saw. I got confused during your approach, because I couldn't tell whether you were going to the victim or circling for position, and then I felt stuck when the tow line came out before you'd made contact, because I had no idea who it was for." She stopped. Her hands were shaking a little, which seemed absurd.

Mael coiled the line in his hands, uncoiled it, coiled it again. "I was rushing," he said finally. "I thought you'd all think I was slow."

"I thought you were fast. Too fast to follow."

He almost smiled. "Go again with me tomorrow? You call out the approach angle."

"And you narrate the tow line."

"Deal." He slung the coil over his shoulder and started down toward the dock, and she followed, the good paddle already in his hand.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
Emily had folded the paper into eighths before she realized she would never be able to read it that way, and now she stood in the back of the synagogue unfolding it while the rabbi's voice carried over the rows of heads toward her grandmother's coffin.

She had written something at two in the morning, three days after the phone call, and it had seemed true then. Now, watching Mr. Tang from the chemistry lab shake hands with her father, she could not remember what it said. The creases had gone friable with rehearsing, the paper soft and splitting along the folds, so that the words sat in white seams.

"You're up after the psalm," her mother whispered.

"I know."

Madelynn had driven her here, had sat with her in the parking lot for twenty minutes while Emily stared at the visor and said nothing. Madelynn hadn't minded. That was the thing about Madelynn; she could sit inside somebody else's silence without trying to amortize it, without acting like the silence was a debt Emily owed and would eventually have to pay down.

The psalm ended. Emily walked up on legs that felt borrowed, and unfolded the paper against the lectern, and read the first line, which was about how her grandmother had taught her to make egg noodles on a Sunday, and her voice cracked on "Sunday," and she stopped.

In the third row, Chris was crying. Chris had only met her grandmother once, at the winter concert, and there he was with his tie crooked, wiping his face with his sleeve. Emily looked at him and something happened in her chest that was not exactly grief. She felt it rise and she pressed it down, ashamed, because the rabbi was waiting and the room was waiting and one did not laugh at a funeral.

She read the rest of the eulogy. She got through it. When she sat down, her hands were steady.

Afterward, in the social hall with the folding chairs and the trays of rational food, the cakes and the hard-boiled eggs, Chris found her by the window. "I have to tell you something and it's going to sound terrible," he said.

"Tell me."

"I keep laughing. Like, at school yesterday, Dan fell off his chair in physics and I laughed so hard I couldn't breathe. And then I remembered I was supposed to be sad about your grandma and I felt like a fraud. I felt like I was doing it wrong."

Emily looked past him at the parking lot, where Madelynn was moving her car to make room for the hearse. All morning she had been carrying the same malaise, a low gray wrongness in herself, the suspicion that her own grief was defective, too small, arriving at the wrong times. Laughing in the parking lot yesterday. Sleeping through the night. Feeling fine, then feeling nothing, then feeling guilty for the nothing.

"Mr. Tang told me something in lab on Thursday," she said. "He does the grief counseling research, before this. He said this psychologist, George Bonanno, studied bereaved people and found that resilience is actually common. That it's not some rare thing, most people manage. And that there aren't mandatory stages everyone has to pass through after a loss."

Chris stared at her. "So I'm not broken?"

"That's what he said. There's no checklist." She turned her cup of coffee in its saucer. "I laughed today. During my own grandmother's eulogy. At you, because your tie was so crooked."

"You laughed?" He looked almost relieved, and then guilty about being relieved, and she watched him work through it, the same arithmetic she'd been doing all week.

Later, when the hall had emptied and the folding chairs were stacked, Emily helped her mother carry the leftover platters to the car. The sky over the parking lot was doing something orange and ordinary behind the funeral home. She thought about the paper in her pocket, its creases and seams, and how she had read it anyway, how it had held.

"Are you all right?" her mother asked, loading the last tray.

"I don't know yet," Emily said. "I think that might be allowed."

Her mother looked at her for a long moment, then closed the trunk. From across the lot, Madelynn honked once, softly, and Emily lifted her hand and walked toward the car.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In her 1997 essay on leverage points, Donella Meadows argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much, while changing its goals or underlying paradigm changes the most.
story:
The sign-up sheet for public comment at the city council meeting sat on the library's front desk beside a bowl of pens that mostly didn't work, and Levi added his name in the last working one because Lorelai had said, twice, that someone from the environmental club should speak. The issue was the proposed downtown parking fee, two dollars an hour instead of one, and the whole debate he'd listened to online had been about the number. One dollar would strangle small businesses. Two dollars would save the planet. A councilwoman had spent six minutes on revenue projections. Nobody had said anything Levi could remember an hour later.

He spread his notes across a carrel by the window. Lorelai wanted him to argue for the higher fee, faster, because the club's position paper said transportation emissions mattered. Ali, who worked summers at his uncle's shop two blocks from the parking garage, wanted him to remonstrate against any fee at all, had in fact texted him a paragraph about customers driving in from the valley. Levi sat between them the way he sat between his parents at dinner, nodding at each in turn and committing to nothing.

Mr. Rodríguez, who ran the donations shelf at the back, noticed him refilling the same page with crossed-out openings. "You keep writing your first sentence like it's a funeral," he said, sliding a cardboard box onto the table. "Sustainability journals. A professor's estate. Take what you want before we recycle the rest."

The box smelled like a basement. Levi leafed through it out of politeness, and near the bottom found a photocopied essay, stapled, its margins dense with a stranger's handwriting. The title mentioned leverage points. The author, Donella Meadows, had argued in 1997 that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much, while changing its goals or the paradigm underneath changes the most. There were rankings, diagrams, a list. He read the list three times. Fiddling with a parking fee, he understood, was the shallow end of something.

He found Lorelai in the periodicals room, but before she could ask about the speech, he slid the photocopy across. "Read the part about numbers."

She read it, frowning. "So you're saying the fee doesn't matter?"

"No. It matters some. Just not much." He heard how weak that sounded. "It's a number. Taxes, subsidies, fees, all the same kind of thing. She says you change the system by changing what it's for. What people assume it's for."

"Which in actual practice means what?"

He didn't have it yet, and told her so. She tapped the essay against the table, thinking, and Ali appeared behind her with his coat already on. "You found the argument against me, didn't you," Ali said, but he pulled out a chair.

What followed was less a debate than a dialectic, if Levi used the word right: each of them conceding pieces until the shape of something emerged that none had brought into the room. The fee was a number; the number was shallow; but behind the number sat a goal, which was moving cars cheaply into downtown, and behind that a paradigm, which was that downtown was a place you drove to. Change the goal, make it getting people downtown without needing a car, and the fee question shrank to what it actually was, a dial on a machine built for the wrong purpose. Lorelai said the bus line to the valley had been cut two years ago and nobody at council had mentioned it once. Ali said his uncle's customers came on that bus, before the cut. They sat with that for a moment, the three of them, the fact of it settling.

Levi wrote his comment that evening at the window carrel, and rewrote it, and the version he finally signed said the two-dollar fee was fine with him but it was the shallowest possible change, and that the council was arguing about the size of a number while the goal underneath stayed untouched, and that maybe the goal should be that people could reach downtown without a car at all. He wrote that he wasn't certain how to get from here to there. He wrote that he was eighteen and had learned the whole thing from a dead woman's stapled essay in a recycling box, which the council would probably find funny. He read the last line aloud in the empty library, quietly, and it didn't sound like a funeral.

At the meeting he waited through forty minutes of glacial procedural business before his name was called. The chamber was half full, fluorescent-lit, a smell of burnt coffee. He stood at the podium with his pages shaking slightly and said what he'd written, and when he finished, the councilwoman with the revenue projections looked up from her laptop. "So are you for the two dollars or against it?" she asked, pen ready.

Levi looked down at his pages, then folded them once and put them in his pocket. "That's the wrong question," he said. "But it's the one on the agenda tonight, so, for it." He carried the folded pages back to his seat, where Lorelai squeezed his arm and Ali shook his head, grinning, already typing something on his phone, and the council chair called the next name.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen.
story:
The library smelled like radiator dust and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on the tables after lunch, and Tyler had spread his things across half of one: a calculus worksheet, a battered textbook, and a laptop open to a mostly blank document titled "History Report." The worksheet asked him to find the area under the curve y equals x squared from zero to three, and he had drawn the curve twice, once in pencil and once in blue, as if a second color might make the answer more obvious. It didn't. The region under the curve just sat there, smooth and smug, the way a shape can when it knows you can't measure it.

He tried what his older cousin had told him at Thanksgiving, which was to chop the area into rectangles and add them up. He drew ten rectangles under the curve, then twenty, and the sum crept upward each time, closing in on some number it never quite reached. Was that the answer, the creeping itself? Or was there a place the creeping was going, a shore it would recuperate on after all that swimming? He didn't have a word for the destination, and it bothered him more than the arithmetic did.

Gianna dropped her bag on the far end of the table and pulled out a biology text nearly as thick as his math one. "Don't move my highlighters," she said, by way of hello. She was working on a chapter about coral reefs, muttering about clownfish and anemones, and how mutualism meant both species got something out of the arrangement, shelter for one, cleaning for the other. She read a line aloud because she liked the sound of it: the fish could survive in the pelagic zone, out in the open ocean, but they chose the reef instead, chose the partnership. Tyler looked up from his rectangles.

"So if the fish just needs the anemone," he said slowly, "and the anemone needs the fish, which one's the integral?" Giana stared at him. "I'm asking badly," he admitted. "I mean, is the answer the partnership, or is it what each one gives the other?"

"That's a philosophy question," she said. "I have a fish question. Yours is a philosophy question." She went back to her highlighters, but she was smiling a little, the way she did when she thought a bad question was actually a good one wearing a costume.

The report, though, was the real pressure, because it was due Friday and Ms. Silva had assigned it in that mild voice she used for non-negotiable things. Twelve hundred words on the history of one calculus idea, with sources. Tyler had picked the rectangle method mostly because he was already drawing rectangles, and he typed "who invented the rectangle method for area" into the library catalog's search bar with low expectations. The results were better than he'd feared. A shelf number, a row of math history books between the economics section and the oversized atlases, and a slim volume with a cracked spine whose chapter headings ran from Newton and Leibniz forward through the nineteenth century.

Donald found him there twenty minutes later, on his way to the vending machines, and leaned over the open book. "You're doing homework in the history aisle now?" Tyler turned the book so he could see the page. "Look at this. Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen." Donald read it twice, moving his lips slightly. "So the guy whose name is on the rectangles, he was basically applying for a job? Like a teaching demo?" Tyler hadn't thought of it that way and found he liked it. A person standing in front of examiners, offering a way of thinking and hoping it was enough to be let in the door.

He carried the book back to the table, past Gianna's coral reef, and sat down with the worksheet again. Something had shifted, though he would have struggled to say what. The rectangles weren't a trick he'd been taught anymore; they were one man's idea, offered at a particular moment, an arrangement the way the reef was an arrangement, between something endlessly subdivided and something whole. And the shrinking widths of the rectangles, the way they closed in on the curve like waves on a shoreline, suddenly seemed less like a procedure and more like a bargain both sides kept. He filled in rectangles forty wide, then a hundred, and watched the sum settle toward nine, though he couldn't yet prove why it settled there or whether the curve had agreed to it or simply couldn't refuse.

Gianna packed up around four, zipping her bag over the clownfish. "Did you figure out your partnership?" she asked. "Sort of," Tyler said. "I know whose idea it was and when. The rest I'm still negotiating." He wrote Riemann's name at the top of his report, then 1854, then Göttingen, and left a blank line after that, waiting.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2010 study claimed 'power poses' raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, but a larger 2015 replication found no such hormonal effect, though people still reported feeling more powerful.
story:
Jesse stood in the restroom behind the camp canteen with his fists on his hips and his chin lifted, holding the posture the way Anouk had taught him, until the door banged and a small boy from the lakeside cabins stared at him from the mirror's edge. Jesse lowered his arms and pretended to wash his hands. The interview for the fall job at Mr. Xu's garden centre was in eleven minutes, arranged during the last week of camp because Mr. Xu came up on Thursdays to buy the camp's surplus tomatoes, and because Jesse needed the money more than he had ever admitted to anyone.

"You did the pose, right?" Anouk had asked that morning, cornering him by the canoe rack. She ran the camp's peer-mentoring program, which paid her a small honorarium at the end of each session, and she took the role seriously enough to hold mock interviews in the craft hut with a clipboard she had won at the auction. "Two minutes, feet apart, hands on hips. It changes your hormones. I read the study in psych last year."

"Which study?"

"The famous one. 2010. Power poses," she said, tapping the clipboard. "It claimed the poses raised your testosterone and lowered your cortisol, which is the stress one. People who held them did better in interviews."

Jesse had nodded, but he hadn't been able to leave it alone. That afternoon, while the others were at free swim, he sat on the bench outside the infirmary with his phone held above the patch of signal by the flagpole and cogitated over what he found. A larger study, from 2015, had tried to replicate the first one and found no such effect on the hormones at all. He read the sentence twice. Then a third sentence caught him: the people in the replication still reported feeling more powerful after the poses, even though nothing in their blood had measurably changed. He stared at the lake through the trees for a while, and then Aiden dropped onto the bench beside him, smelling of sunscreen and defeat.

"They posted the schedule," Aiden said. "You're the only one getting an interview Thursday. Xu asked for you by name." Aiden pulled a blade of grass apart, thread by thread. He had wanted the garden-centre job too, had wanted it since spring, because his mother worked doubles at the hospital and the bus to her ward cost money he didn't have. He had been the one who taught Jesse the tomato staking method in the camp garden, back when they were both volunteers, and he said none of this out loud, but the grass was shredded now and his knee was jumping.

"You should take it," Jesse said, and was surprised to find he half meant it.

"He asked for you. He watched you do the soil pH thing at open house." Aiden stood up. "Do the pose, though. Whatever gets you through the door." He walked toward the water, and Jesse sat with two ideas that wouldn't lie flat beside each other: that the pose was medicine, and that it was theater; that Anouk's confidence in it was borrowed from a study that hadn't survived its own replication, and that the feeling of power it produced had survived anyway. He couldn't make those into one thing, so he pocketed the phone and went to find her.

Anouk was at the picnic table with the clipboard, drafting the text she would send to the mentoring coordinator that night. She wanted the program renewed next summer with a real budget, and the coordinator had told her to document outcomes, so she was listing Jesse as one: a mentee, prepared, employed. When Jesse told her what he had found, the 2015 study, the larger sample, the hormones unmoved, she set down her pen.

"So it was wrong," she said.

"The hormone part was. The feelings part held." He shrugged. "People still said they felt more powerful."

Anouk looked at her clipboard for a long moment. Then she wrote something in the margin, small enough that he couldn't read it. "Feeling powerful isn't nothing," she said. "Maybe it's the only part that was ever in our control." She tore a strip from the bottom of her notes, wrote on it, and handed it to him before he walked to the canteen. It said: "Pose if it helps. Look at him when you answer. If he asks about the pH demo, say what you actually did, not what sounds good. Tell Aiden about the bus money. He won't ask you himself."

By the time Mr. Xu arrived, Jesse had decided something that he could not have stated cleanly if asked. He would not stand in the restroom like a superhero and pretend the pose was rearranging his blood. But he would use the feeling, if it came, the way a runner uses the gun, as a starting signal rather than a cause. He sat across from Mr. Xu at the folding table with the last tomatoes of the season between them, and he kept his eyes up, and when Mr. Xu asked why he wanted the job, Jesse heard himself say, plainly, that he needed the money and liked the work and would probably be slower than a hire with experience, and Mr. Xu wrote that down without any change in his face. Then Mr. Xu asked whether Jesse could work Saturdays, and Jesse thought of Aiden at the bus stop with exact change counted twice, and said, "Could two of us split the week? I know someone who taught me the staking method. He's better with the customers than I am."

Mr. Xu looked up from his paper, and one tomato rolled gently against another on the table between them. "Send him Tuesday," he said, and reached across to shake Jesse's hand.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
Christopher had the keys in his fist before Mr. Brown even reached the porch, and he opened the front door with an elbow because his hands were otherwise occupied, which his mother, watching from the kitchen, apparently found funny.

"He's early," Christopher said.

"He's punctual," his mother said. "There's a difference. And I already handled the disbursement, so don't pull out your birthday money at the door like you planned." She had refused to tell him what the two hours cost, only that it was taken care of, and the vagueness of it sat in his stomach like a swallowed stone. Leo's lessons, by comparison, had an exact price, a receipt, and a licensed instructor named after a chain of driving schools. Leo had passed his test in June and had spent the whole of July being unbearable about it.

Mr. Brown was a neighbour from four doors down, retired, and he walked to their driveway carrying a battered clipboard and a thermos. He did not look like the instructors in the pamphlets. He looked like a man who had come to fix a fence.

"The sign," Mr. Brown said, once Christopher had adjusted the mirror three times and started the car with a lurch that knocked the thermos over. They were on the ring road behind their estate, and a silver hatchback sat ahead of them in the near lane. "When the car in front passes something fixed, you count until you pass the same thing. If you get there too fast, you're too close."

"Count to what?"

"You'll know."

That was all the instruction he gave. Christopher waited until the hatchback drew level with a bus stop sign, then counted in his head, one, two, and only then crossed the same line himself. It felt absurdly simple. It also, he noticed, kept drifting apart from him, because his foot kept leaning into the accelerator without asking him, the way his leg had opinions of its own. He counted again at a lamppost. Again at a painted arrow. Each time the gap he'd been proud of had quietly shrunk, and each time he had to lift his foot and let the distance breathe back open. It was like arguing with a version of himself that hadn't read the same rules.

He tried texting Leo at a red light. my instructor makes me count to 2 behind cars? Leo's reply came back fast: two-second rule. everybody does it, ur guy is just prolix about it lol. Christopher laughed, then stopped laughing, because Mr. Brown was looking at him with an expression that suggested phones and driving had a relationship he did not approve of, even at a standstill. Christopher put the phone face-down on his knee.

"You keep creeping," Mr. Brown said. "Everyone does. It's not a character flaw. It's just how the foot works until you teach it otherwise."

"It's weird," Christopher said, gripping the wheel as the lights changed. "Like I agree with the rule completely, and then my foot doesn't. Two separate arguments going on."

"Which one's winning?"

"I don't know yet."

The silver hatchback turned onto their own street, and Christopher followed it at what he believed was a dignified distance, counting past the recycling bins, past the cracked post box, past the blue recycling bin with the missing lid. He was on the count, he was sure of it, and then the hatchback's brake lights flared because a cat crossed the road, and Christopher stood on the brake, and the seatbelt caught him across the chest, and the car stopped close enough that he could read the sticker on the hatchback's rear window, which said BABY ON BOARD in cheerful bubble letters, and which he had seen a thousand times, because the hatchback was his mother's car, and his mother was turning around in the driver's seat to look at him through the windshield.

They pulled into the same driveway, one behind the other, like two cars that had planned it.

"Your disbursement," Mr. Brown said, holding out the clipboard as Christopher sat with the engine off, his hands still at ten and two, "was a bag of coffee and a promise to mow my lawn. I don't take money for this. Haven't since my son was your age." He tapped the clipboard once against the door frame and got out before Christopher could ask the rest of it.

His mother was already out of her car and walking toward the driver's side, and Christopher rolled down the window.

"Two seconds," she said. "I counted."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
story:
Gavin had spread his geography homework across the kitchen table like a surgeon preparing for an operation he did not know how to perform. Two population pyramids stared up at him, one for Niger and one for Japan, and beside them the assignment sheet asked the question that had been eating at him since fourth period: "Based on the age structure below, predict whether this country will need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years, and justify your answer."

The trouble was not the triangles. He could see that Niger's pyramid was wide at the bottom, a fat alluvial fan of children spreading outward, while Japan's was practically an upside-down Christmas tree, heavy at the top where the old people were. The trouble was the sentence underneath the Japan figure, which reported a total fertility rate of 1.3 and then, in a tone of total innocence, informed him that replacement level was about 2.1. Two point one. He read it four times.

"Who's the extra tenth of a child for?" he muttered to the refrigerator.

His phone buzzed. Nadia, from the class group chat, had sent a photo of her own homework with the caption "why do they need 2.1 when there are literally 2 parents. that's 2 in 2 out. conservation of people." Titus replied with a single emoji of a confused math teacher. Gavin typed back "meet at my house, I have snacks and a rage," and twenty minutes later they were both on his living room floor, Titus eating the snacks and Nadia flipping through the textbook with the focus of a prosecutor.

"Okay," she said. "So in countries with low death rates, you need about 2.1 children per woman to replace the population without migration. It's right there, page 94. But my question stands. Two parents have two kids. Population: steady."

Titus waved a chip. "Some people don't have kids, though. Statistically. Somebody has to cover for them or the whole thing shrinks."

"Then that's not replacing, that's plus-one-ing," Nadia said. "You can't call it replacement if it requires heroics."

Gavin got up and paced to the window, which was what he did when he was either thinking or avoiding dishes, and his mother, watching from the couch, said, "Which is it this time?"

"Population math," he said. "It's a scam. The book says 2.1 is the replacement number when death rates are low and there's no migration, and I'm trying to figure out how a country full of only-children and no immigrants is supposed to take that news."

"Take it how?" his mother asked.

"Well, like, is it a problem? The book wants me to say Japan needs nursing homes, fine, easy, look at the top of the pyramid, it's enormous. But then I'm sitting here deciding that a whole country's future is old people and no schools, and it feels like I'm sentencing them."

Nadia looked up from the textbook. "You're not sentencing anybody. You're reading a triangle."

"I'm reading a triangle and making a policy recommendation. Those are different weights."

Titus pointed the chip bag at him. "You've been an egoist about this for twenty minutes. 'I must personally determine the demographic fate of Japan.'"

"I'm not an egoist, I'm being responsible."

"You're being an egoist with a protractor."

Gavin laughed despite himself and sat back down on the floor. He pulled the Japan pyramid toward him again and traced the bulge in the middle, the wide band of people in their fifties and sixties. "Okay, so here's what I actually think. In thirty years, that bulge is the top of the pyramid. That's the nursing home generation, that's not a guess, that's just arithmetic, people who exist keep existing. So the nursing homes answer is right. But the schools part isn't nothing, because below the bulge the bars are thinner, but they're not gone. There are still kids. Fewer kids, but kids."

"So you hedge," Nadia said. "Nursing homes mostly, some schools."

"Sort of, but not a hedge exactly. More like, the pyramid tells you what's already locked in, the people who are alive, and it hints at what's next, and the hint is blurrier than the lock-in." He tapped the bottom bars. "Whether these kids grow up to have 2.1 children per woman, or 1.3, or 3.5, that hasn't been decided yet. That part's still in play. The old people are certain and the future is a coin that hasn't landed."

"That's a hedge with poetry," said Titus. "But fine."

"I'll take it." Gavin flipped to a blank page and started writing, and Nadia leaned over his shoulder to argue about the word "demographic," which she said he was using as armor, and Titus said he was using it as a scarf, and Gavin wrote on anyway, occasionally defending himself with the pencil.

His mother came over at some point and read the top of his draft. "So what's the number again?" she asked. "For keeping a country steady?"

"About 2.1 children per woman, if death rates are low and nobody's migrating in or out."

"Huh," she said. "Nobody told me that when I was having you."

"You had 2.1 of us?"

"You and the dog," she said, and went back to the couch.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In his 1979 book The Imperative of Responsibility, Hans Jonas proposed the rule: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.'
story:
Jackson set his fork down because his mother had asked, for the third time, why he was quiet, and the true answer was a message he had not answered yet. It sat in his phone in his pocket, from Haroon, sent that afternoon: "You had no right to speak for everyone. Some of us wanted the drone program. Come to dinner or don't." His father ladled more rice onto his plate without asking, the way he did when he wanted to signal that the conversation was not optional.

The argument had begun two days earlier in Ms. Nikolaidis's seminar room, where the senior class was deciding whether to ask the school board for funding to monitor a wetland with student-built drones. Edwin wanted the program badly; he had already soldered two prototypes in his garage, and he talked about the data the way other people talked about music. Jackson had wanted it too, at first. Then Haroon, who rarely spoke in that room, had asked the question that had been sitting under the table all period: who speaks for the people downstream who haven't been born yet, the ones who would inherit whatever they decided? Nobody had an answer, and the silence had destabilized something Jackson had assumed was settled, which was that good data was simply good.

"It's the birds," his mother said now, misreading him. "You're worried about the birds." Jackson shook his head. "It's not the birds. It's who counts the birds, and for whom." His father snorted at that, called it the kind of sentence that sounded deep at eighteen, and Jackson felt his ears go hot and did not say the thing he wanted to say, which was that in 1979 a philosopher named Hans Jonas had written a whole book, The Imperative of Responsibility, built around a single rule: act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life. He had found it at midnight, following Haroon's question like a thread through the dark.

He had not found it alone. After the seminar, Ms. Nikolaidis had handed him a slip of paper with the book's title on it and nothing else, which was her way of refusing to do his thinking for him. In the library the next day, Edwin had found him with the book open and had leaned over his shoulder. "That's it?" Edwin said, reading the rule aloud, then reading it again, slower. Jackson watched something move in Edwin's face, a kind of recalibration. "I keep thinking about the drone," Edwin said. "It's just a camera on a ductile little frame, it bends instead of breaking. But the program isn't the frame. The program is a habit. We build one, the school builds the next, and then nobody remembers asking whether we should." Edwin had gone home and, that evening, written a note Jackson found taped to his locker.

The note said: "I still want the program. But I read the Jonas thing you photographed for me, and I think my reasons were about me, about building something and being seen building it. Jonas says act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life, and I can't pretend I ever asked what the effects were past graduation. So I'm proposing we table the funding vote until we can name who we're responsible to. If you think that's cowardice, tell me to my face. Otherwise, back me Thursday. Edwin." Jackson had read it three times, and it was strange to feel proud of someone and slightly betrayed at the same time, because Edwin was supposed to be the certain one.

At the table, his mother asked what the vote was actually about, and Jackson tried to lay it out as a trade-off rather than a fight: certainty against precaution, the wetland's health against the precedent of surveillance over private land adjacent to it, Mr. Okafor's cattle farm. "The drone is a tool," his father said, gesturing with his chopsticks. "A hammer doesn't have consequences. The hand does." "But nobody knows the hand's reach," Jackson said. "That's the whole problem with new things. You can't see the bottom of them. They sit on a substrate of stuff we haven't examined, funding and permission and habits, and we just start building." His father grunted, which from him was concession, or at least a truce.

Later, in his room, Jackson finally answered Haroon. He wrote that he had not meant to speak for everyone; he had meant to speak for the people with no seats in the seminar room, the ones downstream and unborn, because if the class didn't do it, no one would. He wrote that Jonas would call that responsibility, not tyranny, but that he understood how it could feel like both from the other chair. He wrote that he might be wrong, that maybe tabling the vote was just fear wearing a philosophical costume, and that if Haroon came Thursday and said so, Jackson would listen. He asked for a reply, then deleted the asking, then typed it again and sent it before he could delete it twice.

On Thursday the classroom was fuller than the seminar had ever been. Haroon arrived late and took the seat across from Jackson without looking at him, and when Ms. Nikolaidis opened the floor, Edwin stood first, holding his note, its tape still on one corner. "I built the drones," Edwin said. "I want you to know that before I say the rest." He smoothed the paper flat against the desk. Jackson watched Haroon's pen stop moving above his notebook, and waited, and the room waited with him, and then Haroon raised his hand.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
story:
Brianna had taped her ten studies of windows to the wall of the art shed and stepped back as far as the paint table allowed. Windows with people behind them, windows at night, one window made only of its curtain. Ten works, one theme, exactly as the portfolio brief demanded. Beside them sat her artist's statement, three paragraphs in careful cursive, and she had read it aloud to the wall twice before Josie arrived and read it in silence.

"It's good," Josie said, which was what Josie said about everything, including the camp food. "It's just, who is this person? 'The artist explores the tension between interior and exterior.' You sound like a textbook wrote you."

"That's how it's supposed to sound. Professional."

Josie wanted the statement almost more than Brianna did, in her way. She had applied late to the portfolio program, had no theme yet, and had taken to orbiting Brianna's wall like a moon, asking questions that were really reconnaissance. "What does it mean, context? Like where you made them?" She had her sketchbook hugged to her chest, empty except for two pages of hands.

Mr. Kaminski came through with his coffee at the hour he always came through, sardonic about the humidity, about the espresso machine in the lodge, about the raccoon he called the director of operations. He stood in front of the windows for a long time without speaking, and Brianna, who had learned that his silences were not sardonic but just silences, waited.

"The studies are real," he said. "The statement is a costume." He tapped the page where she had written the artist five times in two paragraphs. "An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist," he said. "It explains the ideas, the methods, the context behind the body of work. It's you. Say I."

He moved on to Oskar's wall of rusting machinery, and Brianna sat down with her draft and a red pen. But the red pen hovered. Saying I meant saying that she had chosen windows because she had spent the spring watching her father through the glass door of the hospital family room, waiting for updates, seeing him only ever framed. The statement wanted ideas, methods, context, and her context was that. She could hide it behind the artist, or she could enfranchise the person who had actually sat in that vinyl chair for eleven weeks. She wasn't sure she wanted to enfranchise her, exactly. She wasn't sure the woman on the page deserved a vote.

Josie had come back without Brianna noticing and was reading over her shoulder. "You could write about the hospital," she said, too quietly for the sardonic Oskar, who was arguing across the shed about whether rust counted as a color. "If it's true."

"It's true. That doesn't make it anyone's business."

"No. It makes it yours." Josie set down her sketchbook, open to the two pages of hands, and Brianna saw for the first time that they were all doing something: holding a phone, gripping a rail, signing something. "That's my theme, I think. What hands do when they can't fix anything. I've been scared to say it out loud because it sounds small."

"It doesn't sound small."

That evening, while the mosquitoes worked the screen door, Brianna wrote the statement in one sitting. She wrote that she had made the window studies in ink and watercolor because ink stains and water moves and her spring had been both of those things; that the tenth window, the one with only a curtain, was left unopened on purpose because some interiors stay private even to the person who lives there. She wrote I. She let the I carry it.

At the final review on Saturday, the visiting reviewer from the city spent four minutes on her wall and asked about the curtain window, and Brianna said, "That one's about not knowing," and the woman nodded and wrote something down. Four minutes was longer than she gave anyone else, and Josie, waiting her turn with her hands portfolio, gripped Brianna's elbow. Afterward Mr. Kaminski told Brianna the statement was the strongest in the group, and she found she couldn't enjoy it cleanly, because the strongest thing she had made that week was the fact of having said the hospital out loud, and it was now in a folder that strangers would read, ungovernable, hers.

She walked down past the lake with Josie, who was rehearsing her own statement under her breath, saying I, saying I. At the dock Josie stopped and asked, "Do you think it gets easier, telling the truth in a page?" Brianna watched a canoe knock against its post, patient, repetitive, not going anywhere. "I think," she said, "you just start saying I and find out."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
The gym at the community center smelled of floor wax and somebody's microwave popcorn, and Maya had eleven minutes to decide whether to quit. She hadn't told anyone yet, not even Rim, who was currently at center court arguing with Alessandra about who got to guard who in the scrimmage. The fall league was supposed to be a contrivance, something Maya's mother had invented to fill the hours between graduation and move-in day, but somewhere in October the games had stopped being an obligation and become the only part of the week Maya could locate herself in. Which made quitting feel less like quitting and more like losing an argument she was still having with herself.

"Maya, you're captain, tell her," Rim called, jogging over with the ball under one arm like a stolen artifact.

"I'm not captain. There's no captain. It's rec league."

"You wear the penny with the number one. That's captaincy."

Alessandra arrived, breathing hard, already halfway into her case. She wanted Rim on the wing in the second half because Rim had hit three shots in a row last week and would obviously be hot again. Rim wanted the same thing, which was unusual, since Rim usually wanted only the ball and the last word.

"You don't get hot in advance," Maya said. "That's not how it works."

"Excuse me. I was on fire."

"You were on fire. Past tense. It doesn't carry over like a bank balance."

Rim squinted at her the way she squinted at salad. "Where'd you get that, the philosopher store?"

Actually Maya had gotten it the night before, scrolling on her phone at one in the morning, from a summary of a study done in 1985 by three researchers named Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They had looked at basketball shooters and found that streaks of made shots were no more common than you'd expect from chance alone. The researchers had called it the hot hand fallacy. Maya had read the page twice, then a third time, and felt something between vindication and grief, because it meant Rim's third quarter last week, the quarter that had made Maya love this stupid league, had been luck. Or at least it meant the streakiness of it had been. She hadn't sorted out which yet, and it was starting to enervate her, this low-grade exhaustion from holding two ideas at once.

"It's a fallacy," she said on the court, in the huddle before the second half. "The hot hand. Somebody proved it."

"Who," said Alessandra, in the tone of a customs officer.

"Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. Nineteen eighty-five." Rim mouthed the names back at her like they were a spell. "Streaks happen no more than chance says they should. So we run the offense. We don't feed the fire that isn't there."

Mr. Quinn, who ran the center and refereed when his knee allowed, blew his whistle from the sideline and said nothing, though Maya caught the small crease at the corner of his mouth, the one he made when teenagers were being teenagers in his gym.

They ran the offense. It was, for a stretch of four possessions, beautiful: Alessandra curling off a screen Maya had never seen her set before, the ball moving one pass ahead of the defense, everyone touching it. Then Rim, denied her streak, stopped cutting. She stood in the corner with her hands on her hips, then began narrating her own openness in a voice pitched for the whole gym. "Wide open. Historically wide open." Alessandra started forcing passes to her anyway, out of loyalty or irritation or some nascent tactic Maya couldn't name, and two of them sailed out of bounds. The other team, a group of dental hygienists who took rec league with terrifying seriousness, went on a run.

Time-out. Rim didn't come to the huddle at first; she stood at the water table drinking with her eyes on the far wall. Alessandra looked at Maya and then didn't look at her, which was its own sentence.

"Maya," Rim said finally, walking over, wiping her mouth. "You're right, probably. Fine. But you know what you cost me? Last week, when I hit those three, my dad was in the stands. First time all season. And tonight he's here again, and you told the whole team the thing I was proudest of was a coin flip."

Maya opened her mouth and found nothing in it. The study was true, she was nearly sure it was true, and it was also true that a fact could land like a door closing. "It wasn't nothing," she managed. "You still took the shots. Someone had to."

"That's supposed to comfort me?"

"That's all I've got."

Mr. Quinn's whistle went short and sharp. Maya looked at the court, then at her friend, then broke the huddle herself, jogging out to the corner where Rim lived. She had the ball by the time she got there.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In France, the directly elected president appoints the prime minister, but the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion.
story:
The town hall meeting had been called to discuss the old courthouse clock, of all things, but the agenda slid sideways the moment a man in a green windbreaker stood up and demanded to know why the town council couldn't simply remove the mayor the way "real democracies" remove their leaders. Justine, sitting three rows back with her notebook open on her knees, felt the room tilt toward something she couldn't name yet. She had come for extra credit in Ms. Yoon's civics class. She had not expected an argument about heads of government to break out over a clock.

"Impeachment," the man said, pronouncing it like an accusation. "That's how it's done."

A woman near the front countered that no, in a proper system the parliament just votes the leader out, simple as that, and the room divided along a line Justine couldn't see. Lea-Rose leaned over from the next seat and whispered that the green windbreaker man had proselytized about this at the farmers market too, pamphlets and everything. Lucille, on Justine's other side, had stopped doodling and was frowning at the aisle.

The trouble, as Justine understood it from Ms. Yoon's assignment, was that the two sides were describing two different machines. In one, voters elected a president directly and the president served a fixed term unless something extraordinary happened. In the other, the parliament was supreme, and the head of government stayed only as long as the legislature tolerated them. The man in the windbreaker wanted the first machine. The woman up front wanted the second. Neither seemed aware they were holding blueprints for different buildings.

But it wasn't that simple either, and this was what had been itching at Justine all week, ever since the research session in the library where Lucille had slid a book across the table and said, "Look at France, it's weird." In France, the president was elected directly by the people, which was the presidential part, and that president appointed the prime minister. Yet the National Assembly could force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion. So the prime minister answered to both, in a way, to the president who appointed and to the assembly that could bring the government down. It was a system wearing two coats at once.

The mayor, at the front table, was losing control of the room. People were talking over each other about recalls and votes of no confidence, terms blending into noise. Justine's hand was up before she had fully decided to raise it. Ms. Yoon, who had been standing near the door, gave her a small nod, the kind that carried more gravitas than its size suggested, and Justine stood.

"I think you're both right," she said, and heard how it sounded, so she kept going before anyone could laugh. "There are systems where the president is elected directly by the voters. And there are systems where the parliament can bring down the government. France has both at once. The president is elected directly, and the president appoints the prime minister. But the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion." She heard Lucille repeat "censure motion" under her breath, quietly, like she was testing the weight of it.

The woman up front turned around, and Justine braced for the dismissal she'd endured in class discussions her whole life. Instead the woman asked whether that meant the French prime minister served at the pleasure of two masters. "Sort of," Justine said, "and I'm honestly not sure where the balance falls in practice. That part I haven't figured out yet." Saying the uncertain part out loud felt strange, like handing someone an unfinished hem and asking them not to tug it. But the woman nodded slowly, and the man in the windbreaker, though he didn't sit down, stopped waving his pamphlet.

The meeting never did return cleanly to the clock. The mayor called a five-minute recess, and during it Ms. Yoon came down the aisle, looked at Justine's notebook, and asked whether she'd noticed that the town's own charter still contained a vestigial provision allowing the council to remove a committee chair by majority vote, a rule from a structure the town had outgrown decades ago. Justine hadn't noticed. She copied the page number down, and Lucille said, "So we're neither France nor anything, we're just a mess," and Lea-Rose laughed, and the three of them gathered around the notebook while the clock over the mayor's head, still unrepaired, ticked its slow and slightly uneven minute.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Mr. Foster had reserved the back carrel for the extended essay students, and by the third period Ethan had spread his life across it: two articles, a highlighted style guide, a coffee he was too young to have brought in and which Mr. Foster pretended not to see. One article, by a team at a large university, argued that later school start times improved adolescent sleep. The other, a single author writing alone, claimed the gains evaporated once you looked at the right subgroups. Both cited overlapping studies. Both called the other's method flawed. Ethan had forty percent of a draft that said, in three different phrasings, "more research is needed."

Campbell dropped into the opposite chair without asking. "You look like a man being sued."

"I have to compare them and take a position. They disagree about everything."

"So pick one. Flip a coin." Campbell stole a highlighter and drew a moustache on the margin photo of the lone author.

"You can't flip a coin in a critical review. You have to weigh the evidence." Ethan pulled the moustached article back. "That's the whole point. Which one weighs more?"

Ludovic arrived with his laptop already open, which for Ludovic was a greeting. He read both abstracts in silence, chewing a pen cap. "The first one pooled a bunch of studies," he said. "Look at the methods. It's a meta-analysis. It combines the results of many studies on the same question, so it estimates the overall effect more precisely than any single study can."

Ethan read the methods section again. The word had been sitting there all morning under a smear of highlighter, and he had skipped it as furniture. The lone author had criticized four individual studies, each one recalcitrant, resistant to tidy conclusion, easy to argue around one at a time. The pooled analysis folded all of them together, and a hundred others, and the noise smoothed out. "So he beat up the trees and ignored the forest."

"Who's ignoring the forest?" Campbell said, delighted, though he was three pages behind.

The second article was sharper than Ethan wanted it to be, though. Its author had pointed out real sins: one study in the pool had measured sleep by questionnaire, another by wrist sensor, and treating them as interchangeable was sloppy. Ludovic shrugged. "Then contextualize it. That's what my sister says her professor makes them do. Put each article in its frame. One is precise about the big picture and loose at the edges. The other is sharp about the edges and vague about the picture."

Ethan opened his phone under the table and typed to his mother, who taught sixth grade and considered herself a scholar of hallway politics: Doing essay on school start times. Which article should I trust, the one that says teenagers are zombies or the one that says zombies are fine?

Her reply came before he'd put the phone down: The one written by someone who has met a teenager. Also you left your physics book in the kitchen. It is being held hostage.

He laughed, quietly enough that Mr. Foster only glanced over, and then sat with the reply the way you sit with a fair point. Everyone in this argument had met teenagers. Culpability for the disagreement didn't belong to bias alone; it belonged to the question itself, which kept changing shape depending on which school, which students, which measurement you trusted. The meta-analysis gave him ground to stand on, but the lone author kept pulling the ground out from specific corners of it.

He started a fresh page and wrote the sentence he'd been avoiding for two days: the pooled evidence favors later start times, and the strongest single objection concerns how the pooled studies measured sleep, and he did not yet know which concern should win. That was not a hedge, he decided, or not only a hedge. It was the actual shape of what he knew.

Campbell leaned over the laptop. "That says you don't know."

"It says I know where I don't know. There's a difference."

"That's the most boring superpower I've ever heard of."

Ethan printed the paragraph, mostly to have something to slide across the table, and watched Campbell read it with his lips moving. Outside the window, Mr. Foster was taping a sign to the returns cart that said QUIET MEANS YOU, ETHAN AND FRIENDS, and underlined it twice.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: According to Acts 15 in the New Testament, a meeting of the early church in Jerusalem decided that non-Jewish converts to Christianity did not need to be circumcised.
story:
The argument started over potato salad, which Anthony considered an achievement of sorts, since his cousin usually went straight for the ribs. His uncle had said that rules were rules, that the old book didn't come with an expiration date, and Anthony, eighteen and three weeks from his first semester, had made the mistake of saying "actually." Now the whole folding table was watching.

"You're telling me a rule from the Bible can just stop applying?" his uncle said. "Who decides that? You?"

The problem was that Anthony had signed up for a first-year seminar called Faith and Argument, and the professor's welcome email had said students would debate whether ancient religious rules still applied in modern life, and that they had to use the text itself. No outside scholars, no podcasts, no vibes. Anthony had read the email four times since Tuesday and had understood it exactly zero times more than the first. His uncle was asking him the same question, in barbecue form, and he did not have an answer.

"Nobody decides," Anthony said. "Or, hold on. I think that's not the right question."

"Wonderful," said his uncle. "The boy's off to college and comes back with non-answers."

Jayna, who had driven him to the picnic because his own car was in the shop, leaned across the table. "He's stalling," she said. "I've watched him stall. He did it for twenty minutes on whether to major in philosophy."

"I switched to that being a backup," Anthony said. "That's different."

Pierre-Olivier, who had invited himself along on the grounds that his own family's gatherings involved more yelling about real estate, was already scrolling on his phone with the focus of a man doing something he'd been told not to do. "Okay, wait," Pierre-Olivier said. "Your uncle says old rules still apply. Fine. But the text itself. You said the assignment is the text itself."

"There's a letter," Anthony said. He was reaching for something, a memory of a chapter his grandmother had read aloud one Easter, the details ionized by years of not paying attention. "In Acts. There was a fight in the early church about exactly this. Whether new converts who weren't Jewish had to follow the old law."

His uncle set down his fork. "Circumcision," he said, with the gravity of a man naming a suspect.

"The whole thing," Anthony said. "The argument was whether the non-Jewish converts had to be circumcised, follow everything. And they didn't just pray about it separately. They held a meeting in Jerusalem. Like a debate. Actual delegates, actual arguing, days of it."

Pierre-Olivier turned the phone around. On the screen was Acts 15, and Anthony read it aloud while a cousin fanned the coals and three aunts pretended not to listen. The letter they sent out said the non-Jewish converts did not need to be circumcised. They laid out a few things to avoid and told them to keep it simple. "It's the text itself," Anthony said. "The early believers are in there arguing about which old rules still applied, and deciding. So when you ask who decides, the book's own answer seems to be that deciding was the process. It happened in a room."

"That's one reading," his uncle said, but his voice had shifted from argument to something closer to curiosity, which Anthony recognized because he'd heard it once before, over whether the金星 the antenna picked up was a planet or a star. "Your grandmother," his uncle added, "would have said that proves the church can interpret, not that the rule died."

"That's the thing," Anthony said. "I keep going back and forth. The meeting decided the rule didn't bind the converts, but it didn't erase it for the people already inside. So it's not that rules expire like milk. It's more that a rule can be a wall for some people and a doorframe for others, and the text shows them choosing which. I can argue it both ways and I honestly don't know which one I believe yet."

"Then argue the one where you say you don't know," his grandmother said from the end of the table. She had been quiet so long that Anthony had half forgotten she was there, and she had not touched her plate. "The letter in Acts doesn't pretend to be finished thinking. Why should you?"

Jayna laughed into her cup. "He's going to open his first seminar with 'I don't know' and his professor is going to weep with joy."

"Or fail me," Anthony said.

"Failing you would be a waste of a good potato salad," his grandmother said, and pushed the bowl toward him. "Eat. Argue later."

Anthony took a spoonful, then borrowed Pierre-Olivier's phone one more time and screenshotted chapter 15 for the drive home.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, 'this.name = name' uses the keyword 'this' to mean the object's own field when a parameter has the same name.
story:
Blake had written the constructor three times, and every time the program printed null. The lab room smelled of dry-erase marker and radiator dust, and outside the window the October light was doing that thin afternoon thing, going gold then grey without deciding. He scrolled up and read his class again, Student, with its private fields, name and id, and the getters he'd built exactly the way the worksheet said. In the main method he made a Student, called getName, and the console offered him nothing.

"It keeps printing null," Ayana said from the next seat, not looking up from her own screen. She had a way of monitoring his errors through peripheral vision, like a lifeguard. "You too?"

"Every time. I'm not even doing anything weird." He leaned back until the chair creaked. Luc, two rows over, was already printing things, which meant Luc was finished, or pretending to be. Luc liked to seem finished. Last year in chemistry he had claimed to have completed the titration while his partner did all of it, and when the teacher asked about the molarity he had prevaricated for a full minute, circling the answer like a cat around a door he did not want to go through. Blake had said nothing then. It had seemed, at the time, like loyalty, though lately he wondered whether it had only been cowardice dressed as friendship.

Ms. Littlechild moved between the rows, hands clasped behind her, looking at screens without leaning in. She stopped at Luc's monitor, then at Blake's. "Null again," she said. "Interesting. That's a very specific null, not a crash. Somewhere, your object exists but its fields never got filled." She tapped the edge of his desk twice and kept walking, which was her way of saying figure it out, it's yours to figure out.

Blake looked at his constructor. Inside the parentheses it said String name. Inside the braces it said name = name. It had looked so obviously correct that he had scrolled past it all morning. He set a breakpoint, ran the debugger, stepped through one line at a time, watching the variables like a man watching two identical twins refuse to say which one is which. Both called name. Both holding something. He stepped again, and the field stayed null.

Then Ayana made a sound, a small sharp inhale, the sound of someone catching a door before it closes. "Wait. The parameter and the field have the same name," she said. "So the assignment is just giving the parameter to itself."

Blake stared at the line. The field's name and the parameter's name, identical, and the assignment sailing right past the field like it wasn't there. "So how do you even tell Java which one you mean?"

She was already typing, slower than usual, testing. In her constructor she wrote this.name = name, and when she ran it, the console printed her test string, clean and unmistakable. "The keyword this means the object's own field," she said, half to herself, "when the parameter has the same name."

He copied the fix into his own file, one line, this.name = name, and ran it. His test Student appeared in the console with a name at last, and he felt something between triumph and annoyance, because the entire morning's null had come down to a single word he had never heard of before today.

Later, walking to the bus loop, Luc fell in beside him with his bag over one shoulder. "You got it working? Littlechild says my version was fine, I just had different variable names."

"You had different variable names," Blake agreed, and heard himself do it, the small smooth evasion. Luc's getters had been fine; Blake hadn't actually seen whether Luc's constructor worked.
